Furthermore, we establish that their wave equations reduce to eigenvalue problems, and demonstrate that the associated quantum mechanical systems possess the same symmetry properties as their classical counterparts. Additionally, we show that the deformation of these systems yields a uniformly noncommutative environment. Building upon these findings, we predict the possibility of Lie algebra-driven decoherence, attributing its origin to the Lie algebra-defined commutation relations rather than a specific algebric structure. In evaluating the potential of federated learning, we developed a convolutional neural network, FLNet, to classify tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes into six types. By training FLNet on data from 13 institutions without exchanging data, we achieved a mean classification accuracy of 73.43%, outperforming a comparable baseline model. When combining data from all institutions, we achieved a mean classification accuracy of 83.19%. Our research demonstrates the efficacy of federated learning in developing reliable and diverse models for categorization tasks. When comparing the performance of models trained with federated learning versus those trained with a centralized approach, we found that FLNet performed on par with models trained on centralized data. Furthermore, FLNet reduced the error rate by 12.5% when trained with a reduced dataset, demonstrating the strength of federated learning in developing robust models through collaboration. Our study is the first to apply federated learning in the field of image classification within oncology. In this research, the performance of digital equalizers was evaluated in a real-world underwater cable network.  A key finding was the occurrence of prolonged fiber transmissions due to chromatic dispersion resulting in distorted signal pulses.  To compensate for this effect, a decision-feedback equalizer was tested but it was discovered that it could be vulnerable to error propagation.  To address this issue, different precoding techniques were examined and found to be effective in reducing error propagation and improving the overall performance of the equalizer.  A particular dispersion-compensated precoder was tested on actual underwater data and shown to significantly reduce bit-error rates.  The techniques evaluated included zero-forcing, minimum mean squared error, and least-squares precoding.  The research provides insight into the best conditions and settings for implementing these techniques in underwater fiber transmissions.  A specific scenario is presented where a 10Gbit/s wavelength division multiplexing signal experienced up to 89.8 dB of distortion over a distance of 5173 km.  The findings are also relevant to the development of next-generation underwater communication technologies.  The data used in this research was obtained from a field trial in a submarine cable network between 2016 and 2017.  The data represented transmissions over the SPARK cable, a 10Gbit/s WDM fiber link that connected Brazil, Spain, and Portugal.  The SPARK cable had a distance of approximately 6200 km, was owned by a Spanish telecommunications company, and managed by a research institution.  The data collected from this field trial was compared to simulations and showed similar characteristics.  The results of this research could also be applied to the development of next-generation underwater communication technologies. This paper proves that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a given field possesses solvability. Additionally, we provide evidence that its nilpotent counterparts hold a more intricate property, potentially related to Lie algebras, although a conclusive affirmation eludes us at present. A method for constructing nilpotent Zinbiel algebras is also outlined, exhibiting a dimension sequence akin to that of Lie algebras, generated by a set of basis elements through specific, definable products. A notable example is derived from these constructions, yielding a 7-dimensional nilpotent Zinbiel algebra with a remarkably similar dimension sequence, mirroring that of its Lie counterpart. A theoretical framework for both finite-dimensional Zinbiel and Lie algebras is then established, based on the properties of their respective bases, ultimately resulting in a proven dimension sequence analogy for the Lie algebra. A counterargument to a previously held hypothesis arises from this proof, and a notable degenerate case for the derived nilpotent Zinbiel algebra is identified, leading to a reevaluation of its underlying structure in light of a newly discovered isomorphism to a 5-dimensional heisenberg Lie algebra. A pivotal role in this readjustment is played by a previously unexplored, custom-generated 5-dimensional nilpotent Zinbiel algebra, proving that both its underlying structure and dimension sequence can be derived from that of the heisenberg Lie algebra, following a specific transformation process. A comprehensive examination of the relationship between all involved algebras, accompanied by a revisitation of our initial assumptions and a demonstration of the diversity within the realm of nilpotent Zinbiel algebras, round out this study. A comprehensive examination of the underlying structure of a particular nilpotent Zinbiel algebra, derived from a 2-step nilpotent Lie algebra, serves as the basis for a significant breakthrough: it is demonstrated that any finite-dimensional nilpotent Zinbiel algebra can be transformed into a comparable Lie algebra, solidifying the previously hypothesized dimension sequence analogy, and further establishing that nilpotent Zinbiel algebras are, in fact, solvable. A concluding reflection on the diverse characteristics of nilpotent Zinbiel algebras, coupled with a reexamination of our initial hypotheses and a demonstration of the richness within this algebra type, bring this exploration to a satisfying close. This paper introduces a deep learning approach known as the Electron Correlation
Potential Neural Network (eCPNN), which can learn simplified potential functions
that accurately capture the intricate electron interactions in complex atomic
systems. Trained in an unsupervised manner with constrained data, the eCPNN model
can subsequently solve for the complete configuration interaction (CI) wavefunction,
thereby enabling the prediction of critical properties such as energies and occupation
probabilities. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this model on a set of highly
entangled electrons in boron-like nitrogen ions, Ni~17+, achieving remarkable
errors of less than ~10^-4 in energy and ~10^-3 in occupation probability. We also
show that the simplified eCPNN potentials can reliably predict results obtained from
more comprehensive CI methods across various energy levels and with larger systems
like the next row in the periodic table, C~18. These advancements hold significant
potential for tackling the high-dimensionalality and non-separability issues often
encountered in many-body electronic problems using deep learning techniques. We
further explore the degree to which these learnable potentials can be interpreted,
providing a preliminary analysis of how the learned electron correlation functions
relate to established physical concepts and might extend to other configuration
interaction applications. We conclude that this initial exploration paves the way
for a data-driven approach to addressing the complex challenges in many-electron systems
and we outline several pathways for further research in this exciting new direction.

Tantalum oxide compounds, with the formula Ta$_2$O$_5$, are distinguished by their exceptional mechanical, electrical, and optical qualities, as well as their versatility in being presented in various forms like crystals, glasses, and amorphous structures. To determine the most stable crystalline form of Ta$_2$O$_5$, we performed a comprehensive analysis using first-principles simulations and Monte Carlo algorithms for structural predictions. Our method involved generating a vast array of possible Ta$_2$O$_5$ structures and evaluating their stability based on first-principles calculations of their bulk properties. We employed the Brillouin zone integration technique to avoid issues with structural predictions, focusing on structures that are physically plausible according to x-ray diffraction analysis. Through this approach, we identified three Ta$_2$O$_5$ polymorphs that are energetically favorable, found at 5 GPa, 10 GPa, and 15 GPa respectively. Notably, we found that the most stable form we discovered at 10 GPa corresponds to the alpha phase, which is the pressure range in which it is normally found. We also examined the tafrite (beta) phase of Ta$_2$O$_5$ and discovered that it is more stable when Ta$^{5+}$ and Ta$^{+3}$ separate into different sublattices, which we termed the "segregated tafrite" structure. We found this to be the most stable structure of Ta$_2$O$_5$ at standard conditions, which is in agreement with experimental findings. On the other hand, we discovered that both the "mixed tafrite" structure and the "orthorhombic tafrite" structure we identified are meta-stable, and that they transition into the "segregated tafrite" structure when pressure is applied. We also analyzed the "segregated tafrite" structure of Ta$_2$O$_5$ at standard conditions, which involves a mixture of six atoms in its unit cell, and discovered that it is composed of two sublattices, one for Ta$^{+3}$ and another for Ta$^{5+}$. We further explored this structure and discovered that it is an anisotropic material with unique mechanical and electrical qualities, which could be of use in advanced technologies. Moreover, a notable decline in factual posts was observed in these regions, alongside an expansion of posts promoting anti-vaccination views, indicating a prolonged impact on misinformation circulation. A survey of Redditors confirmed the findings, with users from the BBB regions displaying a greater willingness to endorse and share information that had not been fact-checked. Neural Machine Translation models have been highly successful in recent years, achieving superior results to previous state-of-the-art methods. However, significant challenges remain when translating languages with limited resources, largely due to the restricted size and accuracy of source and target dictionaries available for transfer learning. In response to these issues, we propose a novel approach to include a monolingual lexicon knowledge base in the training of NMT models. This approach enables the use of source and target language dictionaries during translation, allowing for the sharing of knowledge between similar words and allowing models to learn from data with parallel and nonparallel sentences. We apply this approach to two challenging translation scenarios: translating languages with limited resources and translating languages with extensive resources, and our results demonstrate a notable improvement in translation accuracy. Notably, our approach achieves a significant boost of 1.48 in BLEU scores for low-resource language translation and 1.03 in BLEU scores for source-language-rich-target-language-poor translation scenarios, ultimately establishing a new state-of-the-art in NMT. The code for our model is available online at https://github.com/ghrua/lexicon-guided-nmt. Moreover, we introduce a novel evaluation metric called type-aware BLEU, which measures the effectiveness of our model in translating different word types, further highlighting its strengths and weaknesses. We also conduct multiple system experiments to compare our approach with other state-of-the-art models, including models that use single-source and multi-source transfer learning, models that incorporate a monolingual knowledge base, and models that use intermediate language proxies. The results of these experiments are also included in our analysis and can be found in Figure 1 in the appendix. Lastly, we apply our model to a real-world scenario, integrating it into a live online translation platform used by millions of users every day. The model achieves a significant improvement in translation accuracy, resulting in a decrease in user complaints related to translation errors. We also include the details of the system experiments conducted on this translation platform in the appendix. Ultimately, our approach showcases its versatility by successfully handling a variety of word types, including both common and uncommon words, and demonstrates its capacity to learn from diverse data sets, including parallel and nonparallel sentences. The results of our experiments serve as a guiding light for future research in the field of neural machine translation, providing a clear path forward for the development of more sophisticated models that can effectively learn from diverse data sets, include a monolingual lexicon knowledge base, and include a wide variety of word types in the target language.

Utilizing the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and Sloan Digital Sky Survey, we develop a statistical method to measure the cosmic shear distribution under weak gravitational lensing. This approach enables us to constrain the parameters of a model that includes the SN Ia nuisance term, specifically the residual cosmological parameter $\beta$ associated with the correlation between SNe and weak lensing. Through this method, we obtain a value for the effective residual parameter $\beta$ in a two-dimensional space defined by the product of a SN Ia density field and a weak lensing convergence, integrated over specific mass scales. Our findings support the $\Lambda$CDM model, yielding a value for $\beta$ that is consistent with predictions based on the SDSS data, while also providing bounds on this parameter, specifically in the mass range $10^{11} M_{\odot} < M < 10^{12.5} M_{\odot}$. For the most relevant mass range, $10^{11.5} M_{\odot} < M < 10^{12.5} M_{\odot}$, we obtain the tightest constraint yet on the SN Ia-weak lensing cross term, with a value of $-0.076\pm0.019$. This analysis offers a fresh perspective on using SN Ia data in conjunction with weak lensing to investigate the dynamics of the universe. Furthermore, our method may be adapted for use with more comprehensive SN Ia datasets, such as the upcoming Zwicky Transient Facility and the Dark Energy Survey SN Ia samples. Through this analysis, we derive a new equation that relates the residual cosmological parameter $\beta$ to the standard cosmological parameter $\omega$, which may be useful in evaluating the impact of SN Ia data on future weak lensing cosmology analyses. This study provides a foundation for enhancing future analyses involving SN Ia and weak lensing by incorporating additional data sets, such as galaxy clusters and anisotropies of the cosmic microwave background. Ultimately, our analysis facilitates a more integrated approach to analyzing the universe's structure and dynamics, one that combines multiple observational probes. Furthermore, our results demonstrate the capability of using the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and the SDSS to measure the cosmic shear distribution under weak gravitational lensing, a method that will be indispensable when analyzing the universe using combined probes in future studies. This lecture will introduce stochastic partial differential equations (SPDEs) using the concepts of probability measures and PDEs. We will discuss key ideas such as the definition of a probability measure, the notion of stationarity, and how they relate to SPDEs. Furthermore, we will explore common SPDE types, including parabolic, hyperbolic, and damped equations, and discuss existing uniqueness results for equations that are linear, nonlinear, and defined in finite and infinite-dimensional spaces. The lecture will also cover various methods for solving SPDEs, including pathwise, almost sure, and probability-theoretic approaches, and will provide an overview of the St-Fermon theorem. In the second part of the lecture, we will delve into specific techniques and theories, discussing the Skorohod integral, the St-Itge-Novikov condition, and the fractional damped equation. The lecture will conclude by applying our knowledge to a heuristic derivation of a stochastic Burgers equation. The lecture notes can be found in the supplementary materials. To overcome this limitation, we employ least-squares deconvolution (LSD) to extract photospheric parameters from stellar spectra. However, our research reveals that the line lists used in this process significantly affect the outcomes, as certain lines are sensitive to the chromospheric activity. To investigate this further, we compared two methods for selecting line lists: a parametric approach based on line properties and a randomised approach. Results from both methods showed similar deconvolved spectra and emerged as a robust way to mitigate activity-induced noise. Additionally, we found that using the randomised approach led to a diverse range of line lists that effectively reduced the scatter when comparing different stellar spectra. This method showed particular effectiveness in reducing the scatter under strong stellar activity conditions. To better comprehend the relationship between line properties and the chromosphere, we conducted an in-depth analysis of the line lists employed in our research. Notably, our findings can also be applied to other spectral analysis methods that rely on line lists. Overall, our study provides a comprehensive evaluation of line lists for LSD and offers valuable insights into the selection of lines for both solar and stellar spectroscopy. As a result, we were able to devise a scoring system that rates lines based on their sensitivity to the chromosphere. This scoring system can be a valuable resource for users of the APOGEE-2 and GAIA spectra. Lastly, our research highlights the significance of considering the line lists used in stellar spectroscopy and encourages a more open exchange of line lists among researchers. We establish a new concentration inequality that can be applied to a broad category of discrete random variables, characterized by their expected values and a measure of the correlation among them. This concentration inequality specifically addresses variables with a particular type of negative correlation, often referred to with terms like anti-correlation, negative dependence, or negative association. To demonstrate the utility of this concentration inequality, we provide instances of its application to derive concentration bounds for functions of these correlated discrete random variables. Furthermore, we outline a general method for obtaining exponential concentration inequalities based on a growth condition of the function in question. This method is then utilized to obtain concentration bounds for empirical risk minimization and model selection in high-dimensional logistic regression models exhibiting negative correlation. The model we analyze involves hundreds of features, allowing us to identify model parameters with a limited number of training samples. The key factor in this analysis is the sharp control over the growth of the empirical risk function, which is a discrete convex function. The result we derive for such functions is a key contribution of this research, as it is a significant improvement over existing bounds and is a result of a more intricate analysis. The case study on logistic regression is a second significant contribution of this research, providing a novel application of negative correlation and new insights on the performance of ordinary least squares with weighted loading. The weighted loading is the empirical risk minimizer in the case of least squares, and the analysis of this estimator is yet another contribution of this research. The methodology we develop for deriving concentration inequalities can also be used with satisfaction functions, which is an additional finding of this research. The satisfaction function is a function that measures the discrepancy between a continuous random variable and a predefined threshold, and it has applications in risk assessment. The analysis of such functions relies on the development of a majorizing ordinary least squares objective function, which is a discrete convex function that maintains the same growth properties as the satisfaction function. This study explores the double longitudinal-spin asymmetry in semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering where hadron pairs' transverse momentum is not considered. Specifically, we investigate the cause of the cosine azimuthal asymmetry in hadron production, accounting for the connection between the helicity distribution $g_1$ and the twist-3 dihadron fragmentation function. Using a spectator model, we calculate the interference term between $s$-wave and $p$-wave and estimate this asymmetry at various experiments, including COMPASS, JLab 12 GeV, and the future EIC. Our analysis suggests that the cosine azimuthal asymmetry in SIDIS can serve as a key test for the dihadron fragmentation function. Additionally, we examine the possibility of extracting the interference term through integration of the cosine azimuthal asymmetry across hadron kinematics. This approach is particularly useful for obtaining the interference term even in cases where hadron reconstruction is challenging. Moreover, we investigate the cosine azimuthal asymmetry in hadron production across different flavor types, demonstrating that as the hadron energy increases, the asymmetry value decreases in a manner dictated by the corresponding spin-flavor symmetry. This behavior, in turn, influences the dihadron fragmentation function's twist-3 coefficient at low $q_T$. This analysis holds significant implications for our understanding of the double longitudinal-spin structure of the proton. Furthermore, it paves the way for further investigation of the spin-flavor structure of the proton via studies of the cosine azimuthal asymmetry in SIDIS across different flavor types. This research is pertinent to several ongoing and proposed experiments, including but not limited to COMPASS, JLab 12 GeV, and the future EIC. This work is a direct result of the collaborative ENSI-CAPES/COFECUB project 'Double Spin Physics: Theory and Experiment'. Consequently, we are seeing a surge in interest for the systematic study of double spin asymmetries in SIDIS and DIS at the JLab 12 GeV, EIC, and other experimental facilities across the world. This study is an embodiment of this renewed interest in the double spin physics of the proton, and it is an honor for us to be contributing to this field as part of this project. Implicit relationships among data points, particularly coordinates or features, can often provide valuable information for down-stream tasks.  For instance, the order in which a sequence of words appears may convey just as much information as their individual meanings.  One way to leverage such implicit connections is by using a low-dimensional embedding that captures these underlying patterns.  However, in cases where the implicit structure is complex or finely granular, the embedding may struggle to capture the details, leading to sub-optimal performance in downstream tasks.  To address this limitation, a different approach is to directly model the implicit relationships among data points rather than relying on an intermediate representation.  This is the core idea that underpins the Implicit Tie framework, which we will explore in this article along with a collection of its key techniques.  By framing these methods within the context of the framework, we will also delinate the opportunities and challenges that the Implicit Tie framework presents, covering topics such as multi-task learning to delay the onset of disease progression in graph neural networks and the application of implicit ties to discrete data sources like tree sequences and sets of words. This framework is further expanded by pycommute, a Python 3.x interface to libcommute, offering a more intuitive and user-friendly experience. By leveraging the power of domain-specific language principles, the development of applications that employ diagonalization for the investigation of quantum systems becomes simpler and more manageable, even for complex scenarios involving multiple parameters, interactions, and symmetry constraints, thus providing a useful alternative to traditional in-house library implementations. Initial findings from a measurement of the top quark's spin asymmetry, which would help determine its polarization, have been reported for events stemming from t-channel single top quark production. The data, derived from proton-proton collisions at 8 TeV and with a total luminosity of 19.7 fb^-1, failed to reveal significant differences between observed and predicted event rates for certain top quark decay characteristics. As a result, the spin asymmetry value could not be precisely determined but was found to be, when combined with the most favorable assumption, less than 0.239 or, under the least favorable assumption, less than 0.221. As the accuracy of this measurement improves with access to larger data sets from the LHC, further research into the top quark's properties and those of the Higgs boson are anticipated. Furthermore, this method may be employed as a means of conducting direct top quark polarization sensitivity studies at future colliders. As top quark production rates are anticipated to increase substantially at future LHC runs, particularly those operating at 13 TeV and 14 TeV, this method may be employed for precise top quark polarization sensitivity studies. A thorough examination of this method's sensitivity to top quark polarization reveals that it is highly sensitive to the top quark's polarization when interacting with gluons, which account for approximately 2/3 of the top quark's interactions within t-channel single top quark production events. We have investigated the metallic phase of LaNiO$_3$ layered systems, including single crystals and stacks of LaNiO$_3$ and LaAlO$_3$ layers, using $^8$Li $\beta$-detected NMR and found significant variations in the NMR properties across different locations within a given sample, which can be attributed to distinct electronic states existing within these systems. A more localized electronic state, with an spin-lattice relaxation time that follows the square of the excitation strength, is prevalent in areas further distanced from the LaAlO$_3$ interfaces. In contrast, a more itinerant electronic state, with relaxation times independent of the excitation strength, dominates near the LaAlO$_3$ interfaces and is characterized by similar behavior across all measured locations within a given stack. We propose a model that incorporates both localized and itinerant electron states to explain these findings and illustrate the influence of interface engineering in the design of functional materials. Our research also reveals the itinerant electronic state to be responsible for the conductivity within these systems. We measured the spin-lattice relaxation time as a function of temperature in order to further understand these materials and observed a more pronounced increase in these systems at higher temperatures. We believe this to be an indicator of a greater difficulty in these systems in reaching a thermal equilibrium during NMR measurements. We have also investigated two different types of LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices with different interface characteristics and found that the itinerant electronic state is more prevalent in systems with better matched lattice parameters. We propose that better matched lattice parameters result in a more integrated behavior at the interface and a better overlap between the filled Al $2p$ levels and the Ni $3d$ levels, which facilitates a more efficient transfer of charge between the LaNiO$_3$ and LaAlO$_3$ layers. We have also considered alternative models such as the Kondo-lattice model and the heavy-fermion state, but we have found no evidence to support these models. Our research provides valuable insights into the electronic state within these systems and the effects of different interface characteristics, which will be beneficial in further research into these materials. Our findings are consistent with results obtained through other measurement techniques such as transport, X-ray absorption fine structure and photoemission microscopy. Distributed storage systems rely on replication to enhance both performance and reliability, but ensuring low latency data access requires handling updates without prior coordination. Asynchronous updates inevitably lead to conflict resolution issues with concurrent changes. A specific class of storage systems, known as Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs), is designed to resolve updates automatically, regardless of the order in which they are applied. We develop a novel storage system called Remove-Win, which serves as a framework for storage engines that support CRDTs. Our design is highly scalable, suitable for large-scale distributed systems, and we demonstrate the effectiveness of Remove-Win through a file storage application. Additionally, we contribute an open-source implementation of a key-value store that integrates the Remove-Win design, making it available on GitHub under the Apache-2.0 license. We believe that our design, along with our implementation, has the potential to significantly impact the development of CRDT storage systems. Radio sources with minimal structure exhibit characteristic spectra that follow a specific pattern. This study targets sources with low brightness, assessed at 1.4 GHz, and evaluates how the optical depth associated with radio sources at various scales relates to the characteristics of the sources. Initially, sources with dimensions under 1.5 arcseconds in diameter have a typical optical depth of around 0.23, regardless of orientation. As sources grow in size above 1.5 arcseconds, the optical depth for sources aligned with the line of sight remains steady at 0.23, whereas sources perpendicular to the line of sight exhibit an increasing optical depth. This difference becomes apparent with sources larger than 4.5 arcseconds in diameter, displaying an optical depth of around 0.05 for sources aligned with the line of sight and around 0.08 for sources perpendicular to it. This distinction holds significant importance for source peeling, a process used to remove the FORESIGHT component when analyzing the 21cm absorption spectra. Sources with dimensions above 4.5 arcseconds in diameter should be treated with caution as their optical depth varies based on orientation, potentially resulting in source peeling errors. This research provides a more intricate understanding of radio sources, incorporating their structural characteristics, which in turn will enhance our comprehension of the relationship between radio sources and the absorption seen in the 21cm line. This study also offers a more refined approach to source selection for signal enhancement in radio absorption studies. Furthermore, it offers a more intricate understanding of how radio sources interact with each other, particularly in relation to host galaxies, a topic of great interest. We analyze the wave-generated shocks produced by massive stellar explosions, specifically S-Dor and YSO-type explosions, as they interact with the surrounding envelope. By simulating the evolution of these shocks, we observe how they engage with the envelope and eventually develop into new blastwaves. Our simulations reveal that in massive star explosions, a significant amount of energy is effectively transferred to the generated shocks, primarily in the form of mechanical energy. However, this energy transfer is less efficient in smaller star explosions, and is further reduced in eruptions from pre-main-sequence stars, mostly due to the larger radial scale of their surrounding environments. A significant proportion of the shock energy is retained as thermal energy as the envelope is heated, but this only happens in YSO-type eruptions, where it contributes to the formation of newly heated envelope layers. We introduce the Frame Semantic Dialogue Dataset, an initial collection of data designed to interact with the Bordes et al. (2009) knowledge base, characterized by a range of diverse semantics. However, this analysis faces a major challenge in addressing instrumental influences 
such as particle bunching and resolution limitations which can lead to distorted 
interpretation of results.  This article will review traditional methods used to 
describe such instrumental effects and propose a mathematical framework to treat 
them as integrals. This proposed framework is then applied to the analysis of 
instrumental effects in final-state interaction studies from the BaBar experiment. 
Faithfulness and practical usefulness of this framework are validated through 
comparison with established methods. Furthermore, this proposed framework is found 
to be resource-efficient in terms of computational requirements. Finally, this new 
framework is highly versatile and potentially suitable for treating instrumental 
effects in other amplitude analysis contexts.

suitable for any context where amplitude analysis is performed. This article will

methods and will explore its potential to enhance the understanding of particle 
physics phenomena.

Deep neural network approaches have achieved great success in various AI tasks, yet they often struggle with incremental learning due to memory constraints and the challenge of accommodating novel classes. A highly sought-after capability in AI systems today is the ability to efficiently handle incoming classes with only limited memory, a skill known as incremental learning of new classes. A significant hurdle in this domain is the problem of dealing with imbalanced data, where certain classes have vastly more instances than others, presenting a classification challenge. This paper introduces a novel approach to calibrate the outputs of models learning from such datasets, leveraging a technique called Bayesian factorization to estimate the intrinsic class prior probabilities, thus enabling models to produce more accurate predictions when dealing with unknown classes in the test dataset. This proposed method is then evaluated on a fresh dataset of images called CIFAR-200, known for its large number of classes and instances, with positive results. A further analysis is conducted to study how this proposed method performs on models trained with only a limited number of examples from each class, with the aim of addressing a critical shortcoming of existing research in this domain: all studies to date have been tested on datasets containing an unlimited number of instances from each class, whereas in practice, models are typically trained with only a limited number of examples from each class. This challenge is addressed by designing a fresh dataset of images called SplitCIFAR-200, with the aim of evaluating the performance of models trained with only a limited number of examples from each class. This proposed method is then evaluated on this new dataset under two scenarios: first, models are trained with only a limited number of examples from each class, and then models are trained with more instances from each class, and the findings show that this proposed method continues to produce more accurate predictions than existing approaches in both scenarios. This research further involves designing a fresh dataset of images called SplitCIFAR-200, and the code is also publicly released on a GitHub repository, that incorporates fresh methods introduced in this paper, such as the approach to balancing data when learning new classes, and the technique for evaluating models trained with only a limited number of examples from each class. This work is also discussed in a video presentation at the MMLA 2020 workshop, and two papers that this research is based on are cited in the reference list. A key innovation in our approach involves transforming the mixed-integer optimization problem associated with this challenge into a continuous problem, thereby facilitating real-time solution implementation. To determine the CKM parameter gamma with higher precision, researchers are exploring various methods to utilize different decay branches of charm and bottom quarks in a global fit. 

For the case of $D^0$ decays into $K^+ K^-$ and $K^0_S \to K^0_S K^+ K^-$, they can utilize the difference in strong phase shifts between the final states, thereby reducing the impact of perturbative corrections.

In contrast, for $B^0$ decays into $K^0_S \pi^+$ and $K^0_S K^+ K^-$, the decay amplitude is more complicated due to additional contributions from loop diagrams, mixing diagrams, and tree-level processes.

Developing a method to incorporate branch-level information into a global fit will be the subject of this talk.

We derive the relevant equations for determining the CKM parameter gamma using branch-level quantities and discuss the methods to control the effects of perturbative corrections, hadronization, and strong interactions.

We also use available experimental data to estimate the associated systematic and statistical errors on the value of gamma.

We explore various methods to combine different decay branches of charm and bottom quarks in a global fit and discuss the expected precision on the value of gamma for different scenarios.

We find that incorporating all available experimental data on branch-level transitions will allow for the determination of gamma with a precision of approximately 0.05 degrees, significantly better than the current precision and that of other approaches being explored. 

We estimate that with more data from dedicated experiments such as LHCb and a more precise calculation of the relevant perturbative corrections, the precision on gamma could be as good as 0.03 degrees by the end of this decade. 

We issue a call for further theoretical investigations into branch-level transitions in the context of determining the CKM parameter gamma with higher precision. 

We also provide several open theoretical problems that could have an impact on the precision on gamma and that could be addressed by researchers in the field. 

In particular, we believe that researchers should further investigate the characteristics of branch-level transitions that are sensitive to the CKM parameter gamma and that are also insensitive to other parameters, such as the charm and bottom quark mass values, until a precision of 0.01 degrees on gamma is achievable in the future.

For a regular network of robots, we establish conditions under these constraints to complete a variety of tasks efficiently, specifically ones that can be satisfied by a coordinated effort, and develop a method to calculate the minimum time required to complete these tasks. Kernel methods have proven highly effective in various machine learning applications, yet their scalability to large datasets is severely limited due to the computationally expensive nature of pairwise evaluations. In response, Random Fourier Features were proposed to approximate kernel functions using randomized transformations, thereby enabling the use of kernel methods on larger data sets. While widely adopted, this method has significant drawbacks, notably requiring an unnecessarily large number of features, regardless of data characteristics, and failing to account for estimation errors in certain applications. This article presents an alternative approach to kernel approximation, one that leverages data dependent calculations to reduce the number of features required, while also introducing a method to anticipate and control estimation errors. Specifically, we derive an optimal number of features needed to achieve a given level of accuracy, along with a framework for estimating this quantity from data. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through benchmark tests on both synthetic and real-world data, showing that our data dependent method outperforms the traditional RFF method across a range of metrics. We also apply our technique to two challenging classification problems, namely quasi-orbit equivalence classes and occlusion free classification, and find that it yields significant improvements in performance. Our implementation is available online, under the name KDDFF. While our method is general and can be applied to any kernel type, we focus primarily on the use of our technique with the Gaussian kernel. Leveraging the structure of positive semi-definite kernels, we show that our data dependent approach is highly efficient, with a direct relationship between data dimensions and feature map calculations. We explore the theoretical properties of our method, including its time and memory requirements, and provide a complexity analysis for both batch and online learning scenarios. Finally, we discuss potential extensions to our method with multiple kernel learning and highlight the advantages of our approach over traditional RFF methods in cloud and distributed learning contexts. Our results demonstrate the superiority of data dependent kernel estimation, and we anticipate that this approach will become the standard method for kernel approximation in the future. This paper investigates the Mobius invariant scalar curvature flexibility on compact, conformally flat hypersurfaces in higher dimensional spheres. We demonstrate that when the dimension of the hypersurface is five or higher, we can derive a wide range of conformally equivalent manifolds sharing the same geometric properties. Conversely, if the dimension of the hypersurface is four, we establish a one-to-one correspondence between its conformal classes and the projective classes of its second quadratic form. Furthermore, a regression analysis of massive star data following the collapse of their supernovae fatalities reveals average Big Apple strengths between 0.10 and 0.20 for masses spanning 10 to 50 solar masses. These findings facilitate theoretical predictions of nuclear properties in massive star objects and contribute to a broader understanding of nuclear physics in these environments. Additionally, they provide a basis for investigating other phenomena, such as neutron star properties and the behavior of massive black holes. Moreover, this study introduces three new astrophysical objects in the Milky Way, which can be used as indicators of $\xi$ and its relationship with the Big Apple strength in local environments. A potential connection with the "isospin fractionation effect" is also established, leading to a greater understanding of this phenomenon and potential avenues for its direct observation. Lastly, limitations inherent to the $\xi$-invariant framework are acknowledged, emphasizing the value of further investigations into this theoretical concept. Nonetheless, the Big Apple strength provides a significant breakthrough in the study of nuclear interaction strength across finite nuclei and vast astrophysical objects. It is also interesting to note that this study offers multiple facts about specific nuclei, which can be verified through experimental approaches like mass spectrometry. Moreover, the Big Apple strength enables a exploration of nuclear properties in mass spectra, providing a new area for theoretical and experimental research collaborations. Ultimately, this study propels the $\xi$-invariant framework forward, addressing fundamental queries about the relationship between nuclear interaction strength, isospin, and elliptical deformations in finite nuclei and vast astrophysical objects. In this work, we introduce a novel differentiable module called the Hamiltonian Neural Network (HamNN), which can accurately generate precise derivatives for any input function, independent of noise. This HamNN is an end-to-end differentiable system that can be easily integrated into existing neural network architectures, enhancing their performance in tasks like regression and function evaluation. We demonstrate through extensive experiments that the HamNN consistently outperforms traditional neural network methods and even achieves state-of-the-art results in missing input imputation. Furthermore, we show that the HamNN can learn derivative patterns from data, which is a key aspect that contributes to its improved performance. We believe this HamNN will prove valuable in various applications, especially in real-time prediction scenarios, and are confident that it represents a significant breakthrough in the field of neural network architecture. We are excited to share both the source code and technical details of this research with the community. 

In particular, we investigate how Hamiltonian Neural Networks can be trained to learn derivatives of any function, which is a crucial aspect, and through various experiments, we verify that these models can indeed learn derivatives accurately. We also explore how these models can be used for missing data imputation, which involves leveraging the learned derivatives to estimate the missing values. In response to this challenge, this paper introduces a novel, data-efficient method called the Context-gloss Enhancement Model, which leverages existing lexical knowledge without requiring additional gloss data. This method involves two stages. First, a context model is used to identify potential senses related to the target word's ambiguities. Second, a gloss model is employed to select the most appropriate sense based on the context and available lexical knowledge. This two-stage approach allows the models to operate independently, enabling the use of existing lexical knowledge to guide the selection process. Current text-to-SQL systems are primarily limited to interpreting natural language inputs with the same vocabulary as their trained datasets. This study breaks new ground by expanding the scope of interpretation to include databases with different schema, a challenge further complicated by the inherent disparity between natural language and formal database languages. To tackle this issue, we propose a cross-domain text-to-SQL framework that incorporates an additional task to bridge the gap between these domains. By transforming both natural language and formal database languages into a common representation, our framework can utilize neural network-based models to perform the interpretation task. To further enhance performance, we introduce a joint inference algorithm that allows for synchronized execution of both text and database languages. Experiments conducted on a large-scale dataset demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed framework, with results showing it outperforms the existing state-of-the-art baseline by a significant 5.8% in overall accuracy. Moreover, our approach exhibits superior performance on unseen database schemas, achieving a notable 10.6% improvement in accuracy. Additionally, our framework succeeds in generalizing to new text-to-SQL tasks, achieving a notable 4.6% improvement in accuracy when applied to the SPAD dataset. Furthermore, our approach proves particularly effective on datasets with limited training data, achieving a notable 7.8% improvement in accuracy when applied to the DrivTin dataset. Temporal action detection is focused on localizing actions within a video timeline.
A common approach, boundary-based detection, divides the process into two sub-tasks:
1. Discovering potential action boundaries, then
2. Refining these boundaries by creating action masks.
Current boundary detection approaches often struggle with low IoU scores due to
1. Missing context along the time dimension and
2. Limited consideration of dual contexts (both spatial and temporal) when
   aggregating feature information.
To address these issues, we present a new boundary detection network called
Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN). DCAN incorporates contextual
information along the time dimension and extracts dual contexts in both spatial
and temporal dimensions for feature aggregation. Our network is particularly
effective at boundary detection and contributes significantly to the overall
precision of temporal action detection. Our findings demonstrate that DCAN
achieves state-of-the-art performance on the ActivityNet v1.3 benchmark. Code
is available at https://github.com/Mayneong/DCAN. Leveraging our code and the
insights gained from self-modularization allows us to present a temporal action
segmentation framework called Simple- Temporal Action Segmentation (STAS). STAS
is an efficient, lightweight method that delivers competitive performance on the
ActivityNet v1.3 benchmark. STAS is currently ranked 13th among 59 methods.

This study examines large deviation principles for freely interchangeable and independently distributed letters.  Despite significant differences in letter frequencies and strong dependencies between some letters, our results apply broadly and reveal that typical large deviations follow a straightforward pattern.  Our research also identifies unique characteristics of rare and unusual large deviations,  revealing that typical large deviations are remarkably robust and only slightly affected by variations in letter frequencies and dependencies.  In contrast,  rare large deviations are highly sensitive to these factors,  taking on unique shapes determined by the specific distribution of letters and their strong dependencies.  Our findings are supported by both theoretical and practical evidence,  including examples from the English language.  Our results have important implications for recent research on large deviation principles in language models that assume independent and identically distributed letters.  In an appendix, we discuss an application of our results to estimating compound probabilities,  a problem related to the evaluation of loss functions in n-gram models.  Our results demonstrate that approximating these probabilities using a reference distribution that maintains the same dependencies but adjusts the marginal letter frequencies results in a trade-off between two errors:  one related to the reference distribution and the other related to the specific large deviation event.  This finding suggests that the choice of reference distribution is critical and can significantly impact the accuracy of these approximations.  On the other hand,  for very large numbers of letters,  the specific large deviation event becomes less important,  and the accuracy of these approximations is primarily limited by the accuracy of the reference distribution. Following the success of pretrained models in various machine learning tasks, researchers have been exploring ways to incorporate them into learning scenarios that mimic real-world situations, such as continual learning. Continual learning mimics the way humans learn new information without forgetting previously acquired knowledge. It involves learning new tasks or updating existing ones without access to the data from previous steps. Pretrained models are particularly useful in continual learning for their ability to generalize easily from smaller datasets. Notably, when applied to the continual learning of single-task problems, hyperparameter-searchable models like MoCo have been shown to perform well. However, the optimal usage of pretrained models in continual learning remains an open question. It is unclear whether the cost of these models, justified by their performance in single-task tasks, is still acceptable when learning multiple tasks. In this study, we investigate this question by examining the performance of hyperparameter-searchable models in continual learning of multiple tasks. Our results show that these models can be challenging to improve upon even without using pretrained models for certain scenarios. For instance, when learning multiple tasks from different classes in a classification scenario, our results demonstrate that hyperparameter-searchable models perform no better than a simple baseline that utilizes a single learning rate for all tasks. Furthermore, when applying these models to the continual learning of graph classification, their performance drops even further, failing to outperform a baseline that utilizes a single learning rate for all tasks by a significant margin. Our findings suggest that more research is needed to determine the optimal usage of pretrained models in continual learning scenarios. Recent studies on 64Ni, performed both theoretically and experimentally, shed light on a peculiar phenomenon of shape coexistence in this nucleus. In 64Ni, low-lying excited states and the ground state have significantly different collective structures. While the ground state is characterized by a prolate deformation and likely has a spin of 0, the first excited state, located at an energy of around 1214 keV, exhibits an oblate collective structure and likely has a spin of either 0 or 2. A comprehensive theoretical understanding of these phenomena was achieved through a combination of relativistic continuum and configuration interaction approaches, which reveal that the oblate excited state in 64Ni can be attributed to a driving force of monopole interaction that counteracts the prolate ground state. This counteraction elevates the energy of the prolate first excited state at 64Ni from 1117 keV in 62Ni to 1214 keV in 64Ni, thus providing a key explanation for the observed phenomena in this nucleus. Moreover, this interaction plays a significant role in exchanging particles between the ground and excited states in 64Ni, and an experimental signature of this shape coexistence is anticipated in the transition moments from the ground state. A predictive calculation using an exactly integrated framework for quasiparticle-phonon coupling indicates that the electric dipole transition from the ground state to the first excited state should be below the threshold of 1214 keV, and a current experimental search is not sensitive enough to detect this transition. A further study using a combination of theoretical models and experimental data is advised, with a recommendation to explore other possible transitions or observe this shape coexistence in other isotopes of nickel. Additionally, a study on the quasiparticle-phonon coupling in 64Ni reveals that a collective state with a spin of 2, resulting from a 2-phonon combination, is located at an energy of around 1895 keV, and it is suggested that experimental searches be conducted for this state as well. Furthermore, a study on the properties of this collective state in 64Ni, performed using a configuration interaction approach, shows that it exhibits a characteristic rotational pattern, and experimental evidence of this state can be sought through searches for its magnetic dipole transition properties. A study on the electromagnetic decay properties of this collective state in 64Ni, performed using a combination of theoretical models, indicates that it should have a characteristic electromagnetic decay pattern, and experimental searches for this state should focus on these properties

Approximately nine years ago, Igamberdiev and Jumel created a series of Lipschitz continuous games whose pure strategy equilibria could not be found using queries that stayed within a Lipschitz bound. In our research, we enhance their discovery by demonstrating that in a broad category of these games, including variants of the classic rock-paper-scissors game, including near-optimal variants, and certain extensively examined search games, including Gomes and Shapley's version of the well-known archer hunter game, the Gomory-Huang algorithm's full exploration of game trees yields precise outcomes, while any algorithm that determines a Nash equilibrium with a given precision level must perform an excessively large number of inquiries. This significant decrease in performance holds even when the precision of the equilibrium is arbitrarily slightly improved. We also explore the method by which algorithms discover game tree paths and establish lower bounds on query complexity across broad classes of game trees. Furthermore, we demonstrate that both fully and partially explored game tree paths contain intricate structures, which, when combined with the restrictions they place on the design of algorithm queries, result in the exceptionally high game tree search query complexities we quantify. Finally, we examine the implications of these limitations on the capacity to design and solve bi-directionally optimized game tree paths, and we explore potential extensions of these results to greater complexity levels within the scope of our broad classes of game trees. We introduce a new efficient framework for computing maximum probability explanations (MPE) in graphical models. Our approach uses a compact representation of functions, which we call BFR, and employs two key methods to calculate MPE. Firstly, we utilize BFR to create a quick last-mention first (LF) algorithm for exact MPE. Our experiments show that LF outperforms existing exact MPE methods in multiple domains. Secondly, we modify BFR to solve complex constraint-satisfaction problems, and this enables the derivation of MPE under arbitrary soft or hard constraints in Bayesian networks and logical inference. Our results demonstrate that our BFR-LF approach is highly effective for these additional constraint types, further enhancing its utility across a broader range of graphical models. In this study, researchers examine the relationship between shear thickening and particle collisions within dense suspensions, contending that the transition to shear thickening can be explained by a shift from localized particle interactions to a more widespread hydrodynamic response. By hypothesizing that the thickness of the fluid layer between particles governs this transition, they developed a scalar variable to which it is directly proportional. This dimensionless quantity effectively standardizes the shear thickening transition across various materials, revealing a universal relationship between shear thickening and particle collisions. We employ both legarithmic and numerical methods to investigate the ground states of a spin-$J$ triplon model and find that a twist in the interlayer coupling gives rise to distinct phase transitions between superfluid, supersolid, and Mott insulating states. This phase diagram emerges due to the competition between triplon's interlayer hopping, onsite pseudodelinga interaction, and intralayer coupling. A specific phase solid state is formed where the twist in interlayer coupling gives rise to the phases' symmetry protection. This study supplements our earlier research on 3D WIMP-nucleus collision simulation, specifically examining the velocity and scattering angle of incoming WIMPs as they interact with target nuclei. By utilizing the 3D collision simulation software developed in our previous work, we calculated the recoil angle distribution of nuclei for various initial WIMP velocities. The results show significant variations in the recoil angle distribution based on the 90-degree zero-velocity plane. In regions above this plane, the distribution takes on a form similar to that predicted by simplified 1D simulations, exhibiting a characteristic 1/sin(θ) pattern. In contrast, locations below the 90-degree zero-velocity plane exhibit enhanced scattering at higher angles than would be predicted by a 1D simulation, displaying a 1/(sin(θ))^2.5 pattern. In addition, we explored the relationship between the recoil angle and the energy deposited by the collision, observing that in some cases, WIMPs with lower velocities but higher recoil angles may occasionally exhibit higher energies than those with lower recoil angles but higher initial velocities. This highlights the significance of considering the velocity and scattering angle in conjunction with energy in our search for WIMPs. Furthermore, we propose that implementing a detection threshold based solely on energy may lead to a significant underestimate of the sensitivity of direct detection experiments. In contrast, using a velocity-dependent detection threshold could potentially offer a more reliable method for identifying WIMPs, especially in conjunction with other detection techniques. Moreover, our research reveals that even in regions with low velocity and scattering angles, there may exist higher energy events with larger angles, thereby potentially offering a more comprehensive approach to detecting WIMPs. In this study, we utilized a 1 GeV WIMP mass and a target composed of equal parts germanium and silicon, yet the outcomes are broadly applicable to direct detection experiments involving target nuclei of this type over a WIMP mass range of 0.1 to 10 GeV. A well-known dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. It has numerous applications and its theoretical efficiency has been extensively studied. However, its performance was recently shown to decline in the presence of similar vectors. To move forward, we seek to understand how countSketch's accuracy decreases when the input vectors adaptively rely on previous estimates. Through the execution of novel and rigorous experiments, we find that even under adaptive settings, the current upper and lower bounds for non-adaptive inputs can serve as sufficient guidelines if the number of sketches falls beyond a specific threshold tied to the number of dimensions. Moreover, we establish a tighter lower bound for the non-adaptive setting, reducing the existing quadratic relationship between dimensions and sketches to a linear one. Moreover, we explore alternative techniques for identifying the top elements with fewer sketches. Lastly, we investigate the countSketch mechanism with a new analytical tool, discovering that a specific linear transformation achieves the optimal outcome. Ultimately, this finding leads to a 128:1 ratio of dimensions to sketches as the optimal trade-off, significantly surpassing the existing record in non-adaptive settings. This research is a part of the MOPS project funded by the NSF. Our experiments were executed on the FASERC cluster, a part of the MIT Research Computing Project. Our novel lower bounds were conceptually inspired by the works of Ottaviano et al. and Averbach et al. Our code is available for public use at the count-sketch repository. Our paper was recommended for presentation at the 2022 ICML conference but was withdrawn at the request of the editors due to scheduling conflicts. Due to their theoretical significance, we are re-releasing our findings. Our experiments verified that the current dimensionality reduction techniques can fail miserably even with relatively adaptive inputs. For instance, we ran 512 trials with 128 million inputs in each trial, achieving a 0.0004 error with only 1000 sketches, but this error dropped to 0.05 when the number of sketches was decreased to 10. We further demonstrated that the countSketch technique can handle around 10 million simultaneously active elements with only 1000 sketches, but this number plummeted to just 10 when the number of active elements reached 200. While previous studies assumed the availability of real-time flexibility data, we explore the possibility of training machines to predict this data with accuracy. Our proposed method uses machine learning tools to model energy consumption behavior and incorporate feedback from real-time measurements. By leveraging predictions of this model, we develop a control algorithm that minimizes costs under power constraints. Simulation results using real data show that our approach outperforms traditional methods and achieves comparable performance to strategies employing real-time flexibility data. Furthermore, we investigate the algorithm's performance under various conditions and identify key factors that affect predictive accuracy. Our research provides a theoretical framework for optimizing energy consumption through collective action, independent of specific machine learning techniques. Ultimately, our findings have implications for designing proactive demand response programs. While our algorithm assumes full control over controllable loads, future research should consider how to integrate this method with existing energy management systems. Additionally, future work could explore more sophisticated modeling of loads and the development of tailored machine learning models. Our study offers a starting point for addressing critical issues in the field of smart energy systems. This study examines double Higgs boson production at future electron-positron colliders, specifically investigating how it can be used to shed light on the Higgs boson's interactions that lie beyond the Standard Model. We focus on Effective Field Theories to describe the beyond-Standard Model physics and calculate double Higgs production processes in two contexts: the Standard Model Effective Field Theory and the Effective Field Theory of Natural New Physics. We also consider new heavy scalar partners with masses ranging from the Higgs mass to as low as the TeV scale, as well as their impact on the double Higgs on-shell, off-shell, and in dark Higgs modes. Our analysis shows that a TeV-scale electron-positron collider can efficiently discover the double Higgs on-shell production process, while also being sensitive to the BSM interactions influencing the Higgs decay into bottom quarks and the dark Higgs mode. However, the direct detection of the off-shell double Higgs process at this collider strength faces significant challenges and is unlikely to be achieved by the proposed TeV-scale colliders in the current design parameters. We also find that increasing the collider energy from 1 TeV to 3 TeV leads to notable improvements in detecting the double Higgs on-shell and off-shell processes, as well as the process involving the dark Higgs system. Our research provides valuable insights into the sensitivity of double Higgs production to the Higgs boson's interactions that lie beyond the Standard Model and can be used to inform the design of optimal TeV-scale electron-positron colliders. We conclude by highlighting the significance of incorporating the double Higgs search into the six-dimensional parameter space of the Higgs Effective Field Theories, which can yield additional, potentially observable effects that can be used to determine the underlying physics in a TeV-scale environment. This study is a follow-up to our earlier research published in Phys. Rev. D 103(3), 034026. We have incorporated new data into our analysis, obtained from the Higgs precision working group, which includes the results of the ATLAS and CMS experiments at the Large Hadron Collider, as well as the findings from the NNLO calculations of the Standard Model, which are now available for the electron-positron collider, specifically for the delphi-like detector. The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has obtained precise measurements in two areas, namely neutral B meson mixing and CP violation, as well as in rare electroweak processes occurring in suppressed B-meson decays. This study reviews the most significant findings from these analyses, encompassing evaluations of rare processes occurring in B^0_s and B^0 mesons and estimates for the CKM parameter J/ψK^0(S) and the branching fraction for B^0 decays into a muon pair, with results obtained during the 7 and 8 TeV stages of LHC operation. Furthermore, an overview is provided for the ATLAS experiment's ongoing and anticipated rare B-meson analysis for LHC data collected at higher energies during 13 and 14 TeV stages of LHC operation. Feedback from collider theory is also incorporated in this study. 

In particular, this study reviews the 2016 ATLAS measurements for the branching fraction of the B^0 decays into a muon and a tau pair, as well as the 2017 ATLAS measurements for the CKM parameter J/ψK^0(S). It also includes an overview of the 2017 and 2018 ATLAS measurements for the B^0_s decays into J/ψ and a photon pair, and the 2017 ATLAS measurements for the B^0 decays into a J/ψ and a photon pair. Moreover, this study reviews the prime motivations and signification of these measurements in the search for new physics beyond the Standard Model. Finally, it highlights the substantial contributions made by various theorists in providing solid interpretations of experimental data, in forming theoretical predictions used in experimental strategies, and in proposing new analyses to be carried out with expanded data collection during the LHC's ongoing and future stages of operation. In return, it shares the significant feedback provided by experimentalists on the development of sophisticated detectors and precision data interpretation, ultimately emphasizing the indispensible collaboration between theoretical and experimental physicists in advancing our understanding of fundamental physics.

The development of advanced driving technologies relies heavily on the use of realistic traffic scenarios. Current approaches often employ extension-based methods, building on existing scenes with minimal modifications, but these methods fall short in terms of scalability and diversity. In contrast, starting from scratch to generate fully detailed scenes from basic attributes is a more comprehensive approach. However, this task is extremely challenging due to the intricate relationships among elements within a traffic scene. To tackle this difficulty, we propose a novel scene generation framework, SceneGen, which separates the scene into multiple layers and employs corresponding layer-specific models to produce realistic and diverse scenes. Through extensive experiments using large-scale datasets, our framework demonstrates superior performance in multiple evaluation metrics, outperforming existing methods and real-world scenes in terms of photorealism and scene plausibility. Furthermore, SceneGen exhibits advantage in efficiency and flexibility, enabling the creation of complex scenes with multiple large objects and demonstrating versatility in scene type and size. As part of this framework, we introduce a novel multi-layer grid attention model, which facilitates seamless object relationships and scene coherence. SceneGen's potential is exemplified through its application in scenario branching, a critical component in realistic scenario development, for which we introduce an innovative branching model that efficiently creates varied scenes from shared base scenes. Despite achieving exceptional results, there is room for improvement, as the models' ability to reproduce small-scale details and manage large-scale scenes with multiple medium-sized objects remains a limitation. To address these challenges, future directions for this framework include the integration of high-resolution maps and real-world scene management techniques. Through extensive experiments and qualitative assessments, the generated scenes are shown to mimic real traffic scenarios, align with statistical profiles, and conform to rules governing safe and practical traffic scenarios. Additionally, the model's capacity for adaptability in scenario branching is demonstrated through branching simulations, and the code is made publicly available for further development and customization. As a result of these advancements, SceneGen emerges as a premier solution for creating realistic traffic scenarios. As we explore potential extensions to this framework, consideration must be given to fully integrating state-of-the-art modeling approaches, such as grid-based models, to optimize scene generation for multiple scales and object types. On a Cayley tree, we analyze the Ising model and find novel periodic Gibbs states that are linked to specific polynomials associated with the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model. These periodic states are characterized by unique 'local rules' that mirror the symmetry of the tree structure. We demonstrate that within certain temperature ranges, multiple periodic states exist, and show their temperatures are rational fractions. Furthermore, we establish that some of these periodic states correspond to ground states found by Lieb and Talafin, and that they share the same 'local rules'. Additionally, we find that in certain temperature ranges, multiple periodic ground states exist, and that they are linked to the integers through the Chebyshev polynomials. The dataset comprises a total of 30000 high-quality training images and 6000 evaluation images, and it allows 6400 potential 3D bounding boxes to be defined for each image, resulting in approximately 20000 defined boxes in total. However, the inner disk radius during the 2019 observation was found to be significantly higher than in the 2010 observation, indicating that the inner disk radius may vary and might be controlled by the balance between the gravitational pull and the pressure from the outflowing wind. A possible correlation between the mass accretion rate and the inner edge of the disk also emerges from comparing the time-averaged spectra of IGR J19294+1816 during its 2019 and 2010 outbursts, albeit with a margin of uncertainty due to the binary's unknown parameters. While it is common to evaluate the generated text for its semantic and syntactic quality, the underlying representation of this encoding is often overlooked, which can hinder the model's performance in anticipating the next utterance. This work argues that merely assessing text generation metrics from human or automated sources is insufficient in gauging a model's understanding of dialogue language, prompting the proposal of a new evaluation framework that assesses both the quality of text generation and the quality of the underlying representations used to generate this text. To address this issue, a more advanced ID card extraction method is needed, one that can handle images captured at various angles. To achieve this, we propose a 3D rotation-based image enhancement technique that can convert images, regardless of angle, into a more readable format for natural language analysis. Using this approach, we developed an ID card extraction system that utilizes both OCR and NLP, first converting the image to text and then verifying the extracted data through a set of predefined rules. We tested this system with a variety of images taken at different angles and our results indicate that our proposed method is more accurate than the standard approach using only OCR. Our results demonstrate that these models rely on a diverse range of features found in both basic and higher-level visual properties from multiple regions of the ventral temporal cortex. A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies using planetary nebulae as natural standard candles has been implemented for 25 galaxies within the Fornax Cluster. By leveraging extensive spectroscopic data from SINFONI and MUSE, a comprehensive catalog of 13,000+ planetary nebulae was constructed via automated detection and identification. This method allows for independent distance estimates to bypass traditional scale models reliant on template spectral comparisons, thereby allowing for the direct determination of relative distances between galaxies within the cluster. The resulting distances for the 25 galaxies range from 15.7 to 16.4 megaparsecs, with a cluster center located at RA=03h 39:26.8 Dec=-35:37:05.3, and a velocity field of 1264 km/s for the Fornax Cluster. Notably, these measurements show a 30 kilometer/second discrepancy in velocity compared to CFHTLarge Survey, with additional analysis required to fully comprehend this difference, yet both distance and velocity measurements are consistent with previous studies, showcasing the power of this method for accurately measuring cluster members' properties. Furthermore, by exploring the cluster's member galaxies, a candidate galaxy named FF 88351, with an [OIII] mass of 2.3×10^5 solar masses, has been identified as being likely a background object, while two other objects (FF 14825 and FF 16169) with similar properties to cluster members exhibit distinct [NII] and Hα characteristics, ultimately classifying 3790+ planetary nebulae in the Fornax Cluster. The data analyzed in this paper has been made available on the MUSE3D website at https://www.muse3d.inaf.it, with additional information on the Fornax Cluster available at https://www.icat.org/cat/galaxy?name=for%20n%20ngc%201396. Additionally, a paper on the generalized approach to measuring distances using planetary nebulae as natural standard candles is currently under review and will be made available upon publication. This approach differs from traditional image-to-image translations in that it treats the creation and removal of rain as opposite translations.

The Continuum problem, concerning the behavior of hadrons at high energy, has been a significant obstacle in developing reliable predictions for physical processes involving high energy particles.  To address this issue, physicists need to understand the transition from hadronic, particle-based physics at low energies to the fundamental, quark-based physics at high energies.  The Continuum problem affects calculations of cross-sections, scattering rates, and other process quantities, making it a critical challenge in fields like particle physics and nuclear physics.  Our talk will focus on two approaches to studying Continuum: chiral effective theory and quark models.  We will also introduce the model partnership between these two approaches, founded on the principle that both theories describe the same physical processes but from different perspectives.  This partnership allows us to derive high-energy predictions from low-energy data, a key to solving the Continuum problem.
