Hybrid methods tackling discrete and continuous shortest path problems yield approximations, which can be expressed as the minimum of a collection of subproblems minus their individual solutions. Utilizing duality, we reinterpret this as the maximum of a collection of subproblems minus their minimum, except in cases involving only a single subproblem. This dual formulation serves as a foundation for prioritizing subproblems, with their solutions representing potential errors. Prioritizing subproblems is equivalent to prioritizing their corresponding dual variables, which in the context of flight planning, can be reinterpreted as representing the potential errors in an economical flight path. In this context, prioritizing subproblems is equivalent to designing a potential function that increases with the distance of a point from the origin along a flight path. We demonstrate that in two-dimensional space, the highest value of this function occurs at the origin, and it is achievable. Furthermore, we establish that in three-dimensional space, the highest value of this function occurs at points lying on a plane defined by the x-y coordinates, and it is achievable for flight paths parallel to this plane. This theoretical analysis provides a basis for prioritizing subproblems in a specific scenario involving free flight trajectory optimization. A subsequent section presents a strategy for applying this concept to error bounds in discrete-continuous shortest path problems. We introduce the notion of a pseudo shortest path, which serves as a foundation for constructing an initially infinite collection of subproblems. We then outline a process for reducing this collection to a finite size, resulting in a pseudo shortest path that approximates the shortest path. We also outline a method for prioritizing subproblems, which results in a strategy that prioritizes subproblems in a specific order, culminating in the identification of a shortest path that matches or surpasses the pseudo shortest path in cases where subproblems are triangulated. We experimentally evaluate our prioritization strategy, prioritizing order, on a range of random lattice graphs, finding that it yields nearly optimal results in the majority of cases, with an average deviation of less than 1% and a maximum deviation of 8%. We also apply our approach to a real-world flight planning problem, utilizing data from the FAA's BGLibrary, and observe significant reductions in computation time with minimal increase in error. In certain instances, we even obtain a exact solution. In conclusion, our approach represents a significant advancement in the field of discrete-continuous shortest path problems, particularly in the domain of flight planning, and we anticipate that our prioritization strategy and methods for reducing subproblems will be of use to others

Researchers have commonly utilized the Colemann-Darwin model to analyze plane shocks in an expanding universe. However, this model has limited applicability to curved boundaries such as spherical voids. A new model has been developed to investigate intense shocks in a uniformly expanding universe with a spherical void of infinite depth. The new model reveals that at low amplification factors, the wall has little effect on the shock, consistent with the Colemann-Darwin model. At high amplification factors, especially in voids smaller than a unit radius, the shock becomes significantly weakened, indicating a void of the same size could reduce a strong shock to minimal pressure. This model also facilitates calculation of shock intensity in relation to amplification factor and void size. It further enables estimation of the minimum void size required to produce a given down-stream shock intensity from a given up-stream pressure. Additionally, this model allows comparison of theoretical results with observational data analysis techniques, providing an alternative method for deriving void sizes from observed down-stream shock velocities and up-stream pressures, and thus for mapping the distribution of large-scale matter densities in the universe. A new formula is presented for calculating the down-stream shock velocity, given the up-stream pressure and void size, which could be utilized in future analyses of observational data from X-ray observations of supernovae remnant shocks. This model is particularly relevant as most of the matter in the universe is believed to be housed within such spherical voids, and thus shock waves provide a valuable means of mapping its distribution. A numerical solution to the Colemann-Darwin equations is also outlined, along with a new dimensionless form of these equations which facilitates a broader examination of shock behavior within expanding universes of varying curvature. This dimensionless form enables prediction of how the distribution of matter densities in the universe affects shock behavior, and thus could provide valuable insights into the universe's curvature and matter density composition. A graphical representation of shock intensity in relation to amplification factor and void size is also presented, and could be utilized in future analyses of observational data from X-ray observations of supernovae remnant shocks. A void of the size of approximately one unit is found to reduce a strong shock to minimal pressure, and thus such voids dominate shock behavior. It further enables estimation of the minimum void size required to produce a given down-stream shock intensity from a given up-stream pressure. A new dimensionless form of these equations facilitates a broader examination of shock behavior within expanding universes of varying curvature, and thus could provide valuable insights into the universe's curvature and matter density composition.

A recent breakthrough in algebraic geometry leads to the discovery of a new class of generalized Hermite polynomials associated with Coxeter groups. This breakthrough enables the creation of a comprehensive classification of these generalized Hermite polynomials. Furthermore, it allows for the development of a criterion to identify whether a given set of parameters is valid for a monodromy-free Schr\"odinger operator. This connection between the generalized Hermite polynomials and the Schr\"odinger operator is a direct result of the relationship between the former and the symmetry group of the Fock-Goncharov duality. Specifically, it is demonstrated that both the generalized Hermite polynomials and the Schr\"odinger operator can be defined through the action of the B-type Kac-Moody algebra. Moreover, this definition facilitates the determination of a set of valid parameters for the Schr\"odinger operator by ensuring the non-negativity of the eigenvalues of the corresponding matrix. This approach is illustrated through examples of the G2 and F4 Lie algebras, resulting in the identification of previously unknown generalized Hermite polynomials and monodromy-free Schr\"odinger operators. This work also establishes a link between the Schr\"odinger operator and the B-type Dynkin diagram, providing a visual representation of the symmetry group. The gradual separation of an adhesive tape from its backing represents a steady state of friction, characterised by a constant force required to maintain the peeling motion. However, sudden force spikes interspersed with periods of steady state behavior have been observed in previous studies, being attributed to distinct types of friction present in the sticking and sliding phases. In this study, we investigate the force spikes themselves, identifying them as 'events' marked by force increases greater than 5 Newtons. Upon analysing the events within the context of the overall peeling process, we find that events are significantly more frequent during the sticking phase than the sliding phase, their occurrence being correlated with the duration spent in the sticking phase. A notable finding is that events follow a power law distribution in line with those observed in other systems experiencing sudden, significant changes. In addition, we discover that the sum of the energies associated with these events is sufficient to overcome the average force required to continue peeling, suggesting that these events play a crucial role in the overall progress of the peeling process. A model is also presented which illustrates how events might arise as a result of breaking chains of adhesive bonds that form during the sticking phase, their occurrence being influenced by the rate at which the tape is being peeled. A numerical simulation of this model produces results that align with the data we have collected, providing further evidence for the model's validity. A key implication of this research is that complex systems experiencing sudden changes might be better understood by acknowledging the presence of events that shape their behavior. In the context of the peeling tape scenario, this means that models focusing solely on forces or energies require augmentation with components that account for the breakdown of individual bonds that contribute to the broader energy profile. A potential pathway for future research is outlined, where further exploration of the events present in a diverse range of systems experiencing sudden changes will involve developing a more comprehensive taxonomy aimed at identifying the underlying mechanisms that give rise to these events in different contexts. In the case of the adhesive tape scenario, our research highlights the importance of approaching systems with a temporal dimension using time-based segmentation, as we have demonstrated the presence of a significant, previously hidden component using this approach. In recognition of this breakthrough, we propose the term 'hidden structure' to describe the underlying patterns that become visible when analysing data collected over an extended period in time. Current studies on low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes usually assume independence between variable nodes. This research extends that understanding by examining LDPC codes with degree correlations between variable nodes. We establish a growth rate for the size of a typical error sphere in words, using a glassy random code ensemble that incorporates degree-degree correlations. Our analysis is particularly relevant to the binary deletion channel, a scenario in which words are repeatedly subjected to random deletions. Our findings demonstrate that in this scenario, LDPC codes exhibit similar performance characteristics, with the specific type of degree-degree correlation becoming irrelevant as the code size increases. This discovery implies that any degree-degree correlation has a limited impact on LDPC code behavior, especially in comparison to the significant effect of variable node degree correlations in the erasure channel. We also propose a statistical mechanism for describing degree-degree correlations and demonstrate its relevance to the binary deletion channel. This understanding can be used to design degree-degree correlated LDPC codes, with a demonstration of how such codes perform compared to their randomly generated counterparts. Our results indicate that code ensembles with degree-degree correlations, especially those involving higher degree variables, can achieve the same performance as random LDPC codes, with some codes even exhibiting better performance in certain scenarios. This research provides a theoretical foundation for the study of LDPC codes with degree-degree correlations, with implications for the future exploration of these structures in code design. Building on preimage functors for representations, we establish a cluster character formula for affine and finite simple Lie algebras. This connects morphisms of quantized semi-simple Lie algebras to cluster characters of their representations, extending work by Hernandez and M\'endez in type A. Moreover, this framework enables us to determine the character of a module by analyzing its preimage under the algebra's deformation functor, particularly when this module is irreducible in the Ginzburg resolution. As a result, we derive character formulas for irreducible representations of quantum groups, their superversions, and U_q(POS)_c, extending previous works by Kashiwara, Nakajima, Lusztig, Hernandez, M\'endez, and others. Our approach also facilitates the computation of character tables for finite quantum groups and their superversions. Lastly, we find that the Frobenius-Perron eigencharacter of the algebra under the deformation functor corresponds to the center of the algebra in a rational domain. Additionally, we establish isomorphisms between twisted Yangians, quantum algebras, and their superversions, using the preimage functors and cluster characters. This is reflected in the characters of these algebras and their modules, providing a new perspective on the representation theory of quantum groups and their subalgebras. Finally, we discuss potential extensions of this framework to other Lie algebras and superalgebras. As a reference, we include a detailed character table for the Lie algebra of type D_4(1). The concept of an "external memory algorithm" emerged in the 1960s to describe techniques for optimizing performance in data-intensive applications. In the 1980s, the development of fast random access storage, such as hard drives, revolutionized computing, but their limited capacity compared to modern storage devices could not be anticipated at the time. This paper explores the early days of computer science through the lens of hard drive management, tracing the evolution of algorithms and data structures that enabled efficient data processing during this period. We examine significant computational challenges related to indexing, querying, and sorting under hard drive storage constraints, and discuss key innovations that addressed these issues in the past, ultimately paving the way for modern external memory algorithms and data structures. A specific computational model, the "hard drive model," is introduced to illustrate the underlying storage constraints and key performance bottlenecks that influenced the design of efficient algorithms for data processing. This model is applicable not only to its historical context but also relevant to the present day, given that modern storage devices, despite being significantly more capable, still retain common characteristics with fast random access storage from the past. A comprehensive survey of seminal research works that contributed to the development of external memory algorithms and data structures is presented, covering a time period extending up to the mid-1990s. The Forsage cryptocurrency scheme, considered one of the largest pyramid scams in history, has been the subject of analysis by researchers. By examining transaction data from Binance, one of the largest cryptocurrency exchanges, and information from the scheme's smart contracts, they have uncovered key aspects of the scam's design. The Forsage system consists of multiple interconnected smart contracts that manage various functions, including user registration, investment transactions, and contract interactions. A hierarchical network model derived from transaction data reveals the extensive scale of the scam, involving over 4 million unique user addresses and a massive $2 billion in accumulated dividends, despite only attracting investors through a small group of recruitments. The time it took for a user to break even from their initial investment ranged from just over a week to over 540 days, varying significantly based on the user's position within the Forsage hierarchy. Users at the base of the hierarchy, making up over 99% of participants, typically lost money, while those at the top, making less than 1% of transactions, profited substantially. The time it took for a user to enter the hierarchy below the base level broke down as follows: less than half a second for users who lost money, between half a second and 11.5 days for users who broke even, and over 11.5 days for users who failed to break even. The time it took to enter the hierarchy below the base level for users who failed to break even was highly correlated with their contract balance at the point of recruitment, indicating that users with higher balances at the time of recruitment took longer to enter the hierarchy below the base level. The time it took for a user to enter the hierarchy below the base level also varied significantly based on the user's recruitment method, with users recruited through a referral breaking even and entering the hierarchy below the base level much more quickly than users recruited through a price inquiry. We propose that future optical spectroscopic data will be essential in determining the chemical composition and cluster membership of these celestial bodies. We examine the measurement of the phase in quantum systems with the example of tight-binding models representing light-matter interactions in photonic environments. A comparative analysis is made between different measures of the phase, specifically the Feynman phase, geometric phase, and Wannier phase. It is shown that these measures yield distinct results when calculated using different many-body wave function representations. A consistent geometric phase can only be achieved when considering complete sets of measurement operators, derived from Wannier functions. A protocol is outlined for the consistent determination of the geometric phase in periodic systems from first-principle tight-binding models. Our study is relevant to the evaluation of quantum systems subject to continuous measurement, as is the case with systems undergoing rapid scanning in optical near-field spectroscopy. We also highlight the importance of distinguishing between different phase measures, particularly in the interpretation of experimental results. Furthermore, we discuss the applicability of our findings to systems described by SU(1,1) and SU(2) invariant Hamiltonians, highlighting the generalization of the geometric phase in these cases. A numerical implementation of the protocol is demonstrated with the example of a diamond structure, showing that consistent geometric phase results can also be obtained through numerical integration of the geometric phase curve in parameter space. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between the geometric phase and the measurement of systems, proposing a phase measure called the Wannier-Feynman phase, which takes into account both the geometric phase and the Wannier phase. We show that this new measure provides an overcomplete phase space, offering a super-redundant description of the system that can be measured. These networks build upon the foundations laid by invariant MERA, introducing additional symmetry constraints to encompass systems exhibiting power-law properties. We demonstrate that hyper-invariant MERA can effectively mimic the characteristics of systems described by conformal field theories, yet with a significant advantage, as its applications are not restricted to systems near criticality. Furthermore, we show that hyper-invariant MERA can be employed to devise approximate solutions for specific boundary conditions in the realm of holographic code proposals, such as the holographic Hamiltonian approximation, even though the original proposal was geared towards systems in the critical state. We hope this work will pave the way for investigating systems in motion or systems that have undergone phase transitions, utilizing the hyper-invariant MERA framework. A theoretical analysis of retinal chromophore photoisomerization is conducted, and it reveals that static electronic distortion has a significant impact on the efficiency of the subsequent chemical reaction. Despite this effect being relatively minor in ideal conditions, it becomes crucial when the system is subjected to environmental influences such as thermal bath fluctuations and coupling to multiple environments. In these scenarios, the reaction rate is influenced in an disproportionate manner by the electronic distortion, a phenomenon that could have practical applications in the development of sensory systems. A model derived from a multi-configurational approach is used to study the reaction rate under various conditions for retinal chromophores in protein environments, and the results show that the reaction rate can be controlled through the choice of binding protein. In some cases, the rate can be increased by as much as ten orders of magnitude in the time frame relevant to biological processes, making it potentially useful for the design of advanced sensory systems. The most promising candidate, a hydrokinin derived peptide, is further examined to understand the factors that contribute to the high reactivity, and it is found that the reaction rate can be significant even when the initial state is only weakly populated, a phenomenon that could have implications for the biological function of retinal proteins. The study also highlights the difficulty in accurately predicting reaction rates through quantum calculations, emphasizing the importance of experimental measurement for a clearer understanding of the photoisomerization process and its subsequent chemical steps. Thousands of supergranulation velocities in the near-ultraviolet spectrum of the solar analog star AD Leo were measured over a specific wavelength range and time period following its major flare in 1985.  The velocity data displays a significant daily pattern attributed to the star's rapid rotational period. The velocity readings in certain spectral areas exhibit substantial white-light flare similarities, particularly in the shorter wavelength ranges.  Four spectral regions with distinct velocity behavior were identified, with three displaying enhanced activity during the flare and a fourth that declined.  The outcomes of this study support using near-ultraviolet spectroscopy to study stellar flare activity.  The research also uncovered relationships between the velocity of the star's supergranulation and its magnetic field structure.  A daily velocity pattern common to both the pre-flare and post-flare periods for AD Leo was also detected, along with a reduced activity level in the star's chromosphere during the flare's immediate aftermath.  The duration of the flare, calculated using multiple velocity simulations, was found to be approximately 36 hours.  A daily velocity pattern in the star's magnetic field points, potentially induced by the star's rotational movement, was also found.  The research provides new insight into the physics of a great stellar flare, particularly regarding the flare's duration, and a relationship between the star's supergranulation velocity and its magnetic field.  The outcome of one simulation using a 3D General Circulation Model for the star AD Leo, particularly in its supergranulation velocity, was validated through comparison with actual data from a great flare in 1985. The Cauchy stress operator is a fundamental concept in continuum mechanics, often expressed in terms of the strain energy function via Helmholtz's potential. However, due to the inherent symmetry of the second Piola-Kirchhoff stress tensor, it is possible to formulate a reduced parameterization that maintains isotropic invariance while still yielding an equivalent stress response. This study demonstrates a comprehensive reduction of the linear operator, resulting in a new representation that incorporates only the most essential parameters. Furthermore, we show that this reduced form meets the requirements for a stable, well-posed problem, and it is compatible with existing results on nematic liquid crystal models. Numerical implementation is achievable through an augmented Lagrange method, and we provide an efficient approximation for the reduced operator that is suitable for computational fluid dynamics simulations. Specifically, we analyze the material properties of a nematic Ericksen-Leslie fluid and present corresponding numerical results for different parameter settings. Notably, our results reveal that the traditional formulation overestimates the magnitude of non-trivial equilibrium configurations by as much as an order of magnitude. Therefore, the new reduced operator provides a more accurate stress operator for numerical simulations of non-linear fluids. Our methods are free and open-source, providing a flexible framework for network analysis. This concept was applied to design an optimal quantum annealing process for a particular chemical reaction rate problem, outperforming previous records of solution time. Additionally, the research showed that quantum annealing can still achieve solutions with the inclusion of moderate gravitational influences and decoherence. This essay explores the development of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory from 1921 to 1957, during the tenure of director Pieter Johannes van Rhijn, who succeeded the lab's founder, Jacobus Cornelius Kapteyn. When van Rhijn took over, the lab was working to implement Kapteyn's Selected Areas Plan. However, van Rhijn's contributions were marred by his lack of exploration into the broader implications of his findings, potentially stemming from limited creativity or vision. Throughout nearly his entire directorate, van Rhijn struggled to secure additional funding due to severe challenges including the 1930s Depression, the Second World War and its aftermath, his personal health issues during the 1940s, the lab's distant location, and a governmentally favored infrastructure in Leiden. Lastly, the circumstances that led to Adriaan Blaauw accepting the position of director in 1957, setting in motion the revitalization of the lab, are analyzed in the latter half of this study. Van Rhijn's background and his approach to astronomy and science direction are examined in the opening section, followed by a chapter on his tenure at the lab, and a final chapter on his post-Kabteyn era. Ultimately, this essay concludes with a chapter on the lessons that can be drawn from this episode in the history of astronomy. Some key lessons include the necessity for a clear, far-reaching research plan, the importance of location in lab infrastructure, the dire consequences of insufficient funding, and the value of a strong, supportive director who can secure funding and foster a spirit of creativity within their team. Additionally, this study touches on the lab's contributions to the development of modern astronomy, its involvement in international astronomy initiatives, and its role in training the next generation of astronomers. Finally, this essay provides an assessment of van Rhijn's performance as director and offers some final reflections on his legacy. With this study, the historical record on the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory and its leaders during this period is now significantly more comprehensive and accurate. These identities are particularly useful for computing correlation functions involving multiple $\phi$ fields, where the fields undergo distinct conjugation processes. Notably, our analysis reveals a distinct conjugation hierarchy among the fields, which can be exploited to efficiently obtain correlation functions. Humans naturally experience gait patterns known as "walking states" without conscious awareness, and research has shown that these states are linked to specific brain state networks. However, the relationship between these networks and the individual's gait dynamics remains unclear. Studies on non-human primates have made progress in identifying the brain regions involved in controlling gait, but the extent to which these findings can be applied to humans is still limited. A recent study recorded patients' brain activity using electrocorticogram (ECoG) sensors located directly on their brain surfaces while they performed various tasks on a treadmill to elicit different walking states, including slow walking, normal walking, and fast walking. The goal of this simulation is to identify optimal design modifications that could enhance the leg's stability and efficiency when moving across surfaces prone to yielding. A key finding from the study involves the introduction of a critical speed below which the foot behaves like a stiff object in response to shifting ground, and above which it is overpowered by the sensation and unable to maintain balance. With this knowledge, the design of the foot is modified to incorporate a yielding material that, when tested in simulation and in practice, demonstrates an ability to recover balance when encountering hard ground and showcases improved performance when navigating surfaces prone to yielding. Although previous research has thoroughly analyzed the complex dynamics of droplet electrohydrodynamic (EHD) fans in vacuum conditions, their behavior within aerosol clouds remains poorly understood. This study demonstrates the functioning of a droplet EHD fan when surrounded by aerosol clouds at two different concentration levels, utilizing high-speed cameras to capture the underlying fluid dynamics. Effective communication through language cannot be fully achieved without considering negation, a fundamental aspect of all human languages. Despite being present in every language, negation poses significant challenges to current natural language processing systems. To accelerate the advancement of models capable of accurately processing negation, we introduce CONDAQA, a pioneering English reading comprehension dataset. It demands that models infer the implications of negated statements within passages, collected from a diverse set of paragraphs featuring varied negation cues. Additionally, human evaluators asked questions regarding the implications of these negations and performed a series of challenging tasks: paraphrasing negated statements, altering the scope of negation, and reversing the negation, resulting in distinct groups of question-answer pairs that current models struggle to tackle without resorting to workarounds. Our CONDAQA dataset comprises 14,182 challenging question-answer pairs, encompassing over 200 unique negation cues and proves particularly demanding for leading NLP models. Notably, even the best-performing model (UnifiedQA-v2-3b) managed only 42% accuracy according to our consistency metric, significantly lagging behind the 81% achieved by human evaluators. In a bid to fuel further NLP innovations, we publicly release our dataset, along with comprehensive evaluations involving fully-finetuned, few-shot, and zero-shot scenarios. Our CONDAQA dataset showcases the intricate nature of negation in language and our innovative approaches may also contribute valuable insights to the development of more sophisticated natural language understanding datasets. Our experimental forays into augmenting models with contrarian knowledge, alongside our findings, are detailed in our accompanying technical paper, both in English and in Portuguese. Our code, along with our dataset, is now publicly available for further exploration and to aid the development of advanced NLP models. The COVID-19 pandemic has caused widespread disruption, with numerous countries enforcing strict lockdowns and millions of lives affected. In an effort to cope with the emotional impact, people are increasingly expressing their sentiments on social networks, utilizing microblogging platforms as a means of seeking comfort. Twitter has emerged as a prime platform for exchanging ideas, with users posting diverse sentiments aimed at promoting awareness about staying home and maintaining social distancing. However, there is a growing concern regarding the dissemination of fake news that aims to frighten people, under the guise of promoting awareness. As a result, there is a pressing need to develop accurate sentiment analysis techniques that can differentiate between credible and unfavorable information, promoting psychological well-being and preventing the spread of misinformation. In this study, we introduce an original dataset derived from Twitter, encompassing an array of sentimentated microblogging datasets focused on the COVID-19 pandemic. Notably, each dataset is uniquely characterized by distinct topics, with three notable categories emerging – namely, influenza, coronavirus, and general topics. In an effort to validate our dataset, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of nine cutting-edge classification models, as well as seven state-of-the-art techniques designed to tackle sentiment classification. Our findings reveal that certain classification models, such as decision trees and random forests, exhibit exceptional performance when dealing with complex datasets, whereas techniques like deep learning tend to struggle with similar issues. Moreover, our investigation into the efficacy of diverse features, classification models, and techniques will prove invaluable for researchers seeking to develop robust sentiment classification methods, capable of accurately determining the sentiment expressed in microblogging datasets related to the COVID-19 pandemic. In line with this objective, we introduce an original dataset comprising over 18,000 labeled tweets, encompassing an array of sentimentated microblogging datasets focused on the COVID-19 pandemic. Our exploratory study into sentiment classification reveals that diverse features, such as character n-grams and lexical features, exhibit exceptional performance when compared to sequential features like n-gram and embeddings. Conversely, our investigation into diverse techniques, like deep learning and linear classification, reveals that they struggle with similar issues. Moreover, we are the first to investigate the impact of diverse techniques on the sentiment classification of microblogging datasets related to the COVID-19 pandemic, providing a comprehensive overview of our unique dataset that complements our analysis. As machine learning models require large amounts of data to be highly accurate, there's a growing need to combine datasets from multiple sources. However, when these sources are diverse, as is often the case, standard federated learning approaches struggle to effectively utilize the data. This is because each source typically has its own unique characteristics, such as different data distributions, labeling quality, and storage constraints. In response to this challenge, we propose a novel random walk algorithm to learn from heterogeneous data. The proposed method is an iterative process, where new models are periodically created and improved through interactions with data sources located near the current model. The path taken to create new models is determined by a random walk process, influenced by their performance. As a result, the models created are adaptable to the diverse characteristics of the data sources, and can learn from each other. We evaluate our approach on multiple datasets and find that it not only outperforms standard federated learning methods but also achieves comparable performance with the best existing solutions for combining machine learning models. Reasoning with first-order logic and propositional logic is employed in various 
computationally efficient reasoning tools, including SMT solvers and model checkers. 
Although widely used, these tools lack a standardized format for input formulas, 
which hinders the interchange of tools and obstructions found during applications. 
To address this issue, we propose Alethe, a versatile format that covers both 
first-order and propositional logic and serves as a universal medium for exchanging 
logical information between various tools and the Alethe system. Furthermore, 
Alethe is designed to be both human-friendly and machine-readable, making it an 
ideal format for communicating mathematical findings and tool configurations. 
Additionally, we outline the capabilities of the Alethe system, which includes a range 
of features for managing and navigating complex logical formulas, in addition to its 
capacity to efficiently convert formulas to and from popular formats used by 
reasoning tools. 
Moreover, we highlight the benefits of using the Alethe format, such as improved 
collaboration, better tracking of research, and enhanced discovery potential, 
especially in exploratory research involving the interplay of multiple tools. 
Lastly, we discuss some aspects of the Alethe code, which is openly available, and 
encourage others to utilize the format in their research with reasoning tools. 
We also invite developers of reasoning tools to contribute to the Alethe system, 
making it an ideal format for exchanging logical information between various tools 
and the Alethe system. 
We propose the use of the Alethe format in research with reasoning tools, 
encouraging authors to submit the Alethe files accompanying their publications in a 
specific format that we outline. 
This format will be used as input for the Alethe system, allowing it to retain the 
original input provided to the SMT solver or model checker, along with any output 
generated, such as the final status and the model or countermodel produced. 
This retained information can later be re-examined, re-used, or re-fed to the same 
or different SMT solvers or model checkers, equipped with the Alethe system, 
enabling a form of 'post-processing' of the output generated during computations. 
We believe that adopting the Alethe format will significantly improve the 
interchangeability of tools and the understanding of research carried out with 
reasoning tools.

temperature levels. Our research shows that even without phase separation, temperature

lipid chain orders, thereby influencing protein positioning. This effect is shown to be
universal, applicable across various membrane components and potentially revealing a
underlying mechanism by which cells maintain flexibility and adapt to different

The scalar fields are organized as anti-fundamentals ($\boxtimes_{i=1}^{Nf}\boxdot^{Nc}$) for purpose of symmetry. This enables us to apply a precise method to analyze the phase diagram, mapping out the regions of meta-stable Higgs phases for various combinations of Nc and Nf. Notably, we discover that Higgs phases are consistently found when Nf is greater than 1, and that this condition applies across all symmetric group transformations. Additionally, we investigate the critical behavior at the phase transition points between the Higgs phase and the confining phase for both even and odd Nc values, utilizing Monte Carlo simulations to collect data on the critical exponents. Our analysis indicates that all critical exponents follow the predicted Ising universal values when Nf is 2, and that they conform to the predicted values for the 3D Coulomb phase when Nf is greater than 2. Conversely, we observe non-universal, gauge-theory specific values when Nf is 3. This variety arises due to the competition for symmetry breaking between the gauge theory and the fundamental representations within the scalar field. A thorough analysis of the symmetry breaking is included in the analysis of the phase diagram for both even and odd Nc values, along with a discussion of the implications this has for the existence of stable Higgs phases in lattice constructions. A method is presented for ensuring Higgs phase stability in practice, involving the application of a mass term to the pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone boson that arises from the symmetry breaking. This allows us to recover the true Higgs branch at the cost of rotating it within the multi-dimensional parameter space. A comparison is drawn between this approach and the established methods of mass pinning, and evidence is presented that pinning the Higgs branch along this new direction could yield more robust results. A method is described for using Monte Carlo simulations to recover the true Higgs branch, and the results obtained from this process are presented in the form of images of the phase diagram for different combinations of Nc and Nf. By directly inverting the relation between the potentials, we obtain a closed system of equations that can be solved through a successive approximation technique. This enables us to find an accurate solution for the mass function of the star, given a given surface density, in a manner that compensates for the pressure at the boundary. Furthermore, we develop a method for calculating the Hartle-Thorne approximation and identify specific conditions under which it becomes applicable. Moreover, we derive a key inequality governing the relation between the gravitational and surface densities of the star, given its mass density and pressure at the boundary, thereby providing a physical interpretation of the anisotropic Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations. This involves exploring the possible range of values of the equation of state parameter for both fluids, subject to the constraints of relativistic stability, alongside an examination of the effects of pressure anisotropy on the interior structure of the star. Finally, we establish an isothermality condition that must be satisfied for the star's mass function to remain consistent with its temperature distribution. This condition, in turn, leads to a re-derived equation of state for one of the fluids, revealing the relationship between this fluid's pressure and density. Galactic mergers significantly shape galaxy evolution, especially those occurring during the present-day universe where one-third of galaxy pairs exhibit mass ratios of 1:4 or closer. This study initiates a series of articles to examine how magnetic fields affect the impact of galaxy mergers, focusing here on the effects on disk galaxies. By incorporating a galactic magnetic field similar to that of the Milky Way, this study uses high-resolution simulations to explore the effects of galaxy mergers in ideal magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) within the context of the standard $\Lambda$CDM cosmology. The ideal MHD simulations demonstrate that a strong galactic magnetic field robustly resists the dissolution of gas and stellar disks during major mergers, thereby preventing disk destruction. Additionally, this study finds that a strong magnetic field influences the structure and stability of gas and stellar disks throughout the merger process, especially when encountering the shock waves produced during galaxy collisions. Furthermore, this study finds that a strong magnetic field can also impact the formation of bars and central mass concentrations. Bar formation is facilitated in ideal MHD simulations, especially in mergers where the primary component falls short of a head-on collision. Central mass concentrations form in both ideal and real MHD simulations, especially in collisions that are only slightly non-head-on. Nonetheless, in head-on collisions, the contrast between ideal and real MHD simulations is evident, with ideal MHD producing a more substantial central mass concentration than real MHD. This study finds that a strong galactic magnetic field enhances the stability of gas disks throughout the merger process, whereas the behavior of stellar disks is governed by the bar formation facilitated by the magnetic field in ideal MHD, as well as magnetic dissipation in real MHD. Ancient celestial detectors, or "paleo-detectors," offer a distinctive means of detecting dark matter. Unlike conventional detectors, they employ nuclear reactions between dark matter particles and ancient targets, such as nitrogen and oxygen, which were present in massive amounts throughout the universe. While the reaction rates are typically low, the availability of large amounts of ancient targets can significantly increase the detection potential. Our analysis evaluates the effectiveness of paleo-detectors for detecting dark matter across a broad spectrum of masses spanning 10 kiloelectronvolts to one million electronvolts. Depending on the characteristics of the dark matter particles, we find that current-generation paleo-detectors can yield competent detection results for mass ranges between 50 kiloelectronvolts to one million electronvolts. Moreover, we propose an enhanced detection strategy that minimizes target isotopic impurities to below one part in ten billion, which could further enhance the detection capacity by a factor of one hundred for mass ranges between 10 kiloelectronvolts to 50 kiloelectronvolts. This improved detection method can potentially detect dark matter mass ranges below 10 kiloeelectronvolts, which current theoretical models consider highly plausible. By implementing this strategy, the effective detection limit for paleo-detectors can match that of conventional detectors, such as direct detection experiments, for mass ranges between 10 kiloelectronvolts to 100 gigaelectronvolts. For masses below 100 gigaelectronvolts, the achievable reaction rates with paleo-detectors outperform those of conventional detectors by two to four orders of magnitude. Furthermore, we highlight the scientific implications of detecting dark matter with paleo-detectors, which can verify the integrity of dark matter models by yielding measurable reaction rates in mass ranges considered by theoretical models, such as below 10 kiloelectronvolts, and above one million electronvolts. This perspective has been expressed through various formulations of the square rule, which suggests that the inequality of income should be no greater than the sum of the inequalities of chance and the inequalities of other factors. We examine how these ideas relate to each other and to the principle of risk aversion, before moving on to assess them through empirical data. Our analysis indicates that the co-efficient of the square rule is significantly lower than the degree of risk aversion typically exhibited by individuals, implying that people's incomes are not adjusted by enough when they are affected by chance rather than other factors. The marginally employed sector of the population is found to be particularly vulnerable to this, suggesting that their income inequality is set at an unfairly high price due to a failure of income redistribution enough. We use this analysis to support the case for increasing income support during periods of low income and for introducing measures that aim to reduce income inequality directly. Our investigation reveals that single-particle entanglement can result in a unique, nonlocal phenomenon called single-particle steering. In order to illustrate this concept, we utilize a well-known entanglement scenario - the single-particle entanglement existing between two qubits. Our analysis demonstrates that the single-particle state of one qubit can be used to affect the oscillating state of the other qubit, a effect that cannot be achieved through classical means. Furthermore, we show that this nonlocal impact can be observed even when the single qubit is not itself affected by the operation performed on the other qubit. This finding highlights a distinct advantage of using single-qubit states over two-qubit entangled states, which can sometimes exhibit nonlocal behavior that is not unique to single-qubit states. As such, our research suggests that single-qubit states hold significant value in the development of nonlocal information processing technologies. Our analysis also provides a method for identifying single-qubit states that can produce the unique effect of single-particle steering. Furthermore, our research indicates that single-qubit steering is not merely a consequence of single-qubit entanglement, but rather a distinct phenomenon that can arise from either entanglement or the appropriate mixture of separation and correlation. Our investigation also reveals that the unique, nonlocal effect of single-particle steering can result in the generation of a single-qubit state that is not reachable through classical means, demonstrating the unique value of single-qubit states in nonlocal information processing. Our research further demonstrates that the unique, nonlocal effect of single-particle steering can arise from either the entanglement or the suitable mixture of separation and correlation in a single-qubit state, a finding that provides a deeper understanding of the distinct characteristics of single-qubit states. Our analysis also provides a demonstration of the unique, nonlocal effect of single-particle steering in optical systems, as well as a discussion on the distinct implications of this effect on single-qubit states as compared to the effect of steering on two-qubit entangled states, revealing that single-qubit states hold unique value in the development of nonlocal information processing technologies. Using high-level abstracts from Wikipedia articles, our research creates a unique data set that maps concepts to their definitions and tracks the evolution of knowledge across various subjects.  By combining this data set with global productivity indicators, we identify intriguing disparities between regions that are highly productive but lack knowledge, along with areas that possess vast knowledge but struggle with productivity.  Our findings also reveal that the global distribution of knowledge is uneven, with certain subjects dominating the global landscape.  Finally, we uncover the difficult task of pinpointing the most influential knowledge areas, especially in complex cross-disciplinary fields.  To tackle this challenge, we develop an innovative method that uses a neural network to rate the importance of concepts within a specific area.  By applying this approach, we discover that the knowledge areas with the highest impact tend to be those that have a clear, definitive understanding, such as the concept of gravity.  On the other hand, complex concepts like justice or morality are more difficult to grasp and measure. We investigate the interaction between a two-dimensional semiconductor bilayer, serving as a quantum well, and a quantized magnetic field. This system possesses a gapless spectrum and is characterized by an invariant, the Chern number, which can be modified to induce topological phases. Notably, the presence of topological edge modes enables us to design a topological waveguide. By coupling the semiconductor bilayer to a microcavity, we examine the impact on edge modes due to two-dimensional excitons. We find that waveguide modes exhibit both edge mode and exciton-localized modes, depending on the parameter, and can switch between an edge mode and a cavity mode with the variation of a external magnetic field. This transition is accompanied by a change in phase and a difference in helicity, representing a topological non-trivial phase transition. The combination of topological edge modes and exciton-localized modes may lead to the observation of non-trivial topological phases in photonic systems. We propose feasible experiments to verify our theoretical predictions with current technology. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three to four times faster than the original versions.
TextWorldExpress boasts substantial improvements in performance, boasting the ability to process over one million actions per second on a single GPU, without compromising on difficulty or fidelity. This enhanced performance comes at the relatively low cost of adding 5-10% to total memory requirements, which is further broken down by memory type in our analysis. With the potential to host more sophisticated tests, TextWorldExpress is made openly available for the broader community to utilize. A thorough evaluation of TextWorldExpress, including comparative performance data with the original games, is also conducted as part of our research. Interestingly, our studies reveal that existing state-of-the-art virtual agents exhibit noticeable struggles with efficiently exploring text-based games, often failing to take advantage of increased processing speeds. As such, there is a significant opportunity for the development of advanced optimization strategies that can fully capitalize on the enhanced processing capabilities of simulated games like TextWorldExpress. A newly introduced metric called exploration efficiency is introduced to better assess the performance of virtual agents in text-based games, offering a more nuanced understanding of existing results and concrete goals for future improvement. Two notable methods for enhancing exploration efficiency in text games are proposed, along with early proof of concept results for both methods. Furthermore, the source code for TextWorldExpress has been made openly available for the community to use. With the potential to host more complex text games at higher processing speeds, this simulation platform is available for all researchers and virtual agent developers to utilize. A comprehensive evaluation of virtual agents is also conducted as part of our research, further highlighting the utility of TextWorldExpress as a reliable, performance-standard benchmark for the community. With the source code available for TextWorldExpress, we also introduce a new standard for publishing text games, emphasizing the importance of publishing both the description of the game setup and the actual implementation of the game. This is to ensure that the performance of virtual agents is being evaluated fairly, based on actual implementation rather than deceptive game descriptions. This new publishing standard is designed to provide a clear, consistent framework for comparing the performance of different virtual agents

We investigate the nitrogen vacancy center in diamond under elevated temperatures, examining how spatial uniformity and spectroscopic properties are affected by heat.  To achieve this, we develop a temperature-controlled diamond fluorescence spectroscopy technique, allowing us to precisely measure temperature distributions and obtain high-quality spectra up to 400 Kelvin.  At higher temperatures, a significant increase in the nitrogen vacancy center valence state splitting becomes apparent, alongside a rise in radiative state decay rates.  Interestingly, the initial absence of a thermal gradient within the diamond results in a seemingly anomalous, unrestrained increase in decay rate with temperature.  However, the inception of thermal gradient within the diamond leads to a normalization of this observation, as the decay rate returns to its initial, non-temperature-dependent state.  The enhanced diffusion of diamond's surrounding lattice at higher temperatures is proposed as the causal factor for the observed splitting increase, which is corroborated by calculations.  In contrast, the rise in decay rates with temperature is accounted for by a combination of direct and indirect interactions with the diamond's surroundings, mediated through its vibrational modes.  The Nilsson-Whitehouse model, originally designed for optical interferometry, is adapted to interpret our findings on a microscopic level.  This research provides valuable insights for utilizing the nitrogen vacancy center in diamond in high-temperature environments, particularly in optical readout applications of diamond-based quantum sensors.  To this end, we propose a technique for enhancing the sensitivity of this type of sensors in high-temperature, low-light intensity settings.  Our study is also relevant to the development of temperature-dependent quantum simulations using the nitrogen vacancy center in diamond, as it offers a precise temperature control system along with a temperature scale that can support multi-state interactions in this system.  Furthermore, our study provides a temperature control methodology that can be applied across a broad spectrum of diamond-based research. A key discovery reveals that a specific inhibitory neuron plays a significant role in both learning and performing the task, demonstrating how a single biological neuron can fulfill the function of multiple controllers in a non-trivial task. A new implementation of the Hartree-Fock (HF) method has been developed to efficiently achieve robust convergence for well-behaved central potentials. The method converts HF equations into a generalized eigenvalue problem by using a B-spline basis in a finite-size box and incrementally increases the strength of electron-electron interactions. The explosive synchronization phenomenon occurs when a population of oscillators transitions from asynchronous to perfectly synchronized behavior without the development of a desynchronized phase. We have established a comprehensive criteria for this phenomenon to occur, based on the distribution of oscillator phase differences. This criteria is applicable to a wide variety of oscillator models and can be used to map their dynamics. We have specifically examined and analyzed several of the commonly studied oscillator models, such as the Kuramoto, Rossler, and Hindmarsh-Rose models, as well as nonlocal interactions and phase transitions. Our analysis confirms that the explosive synchronization criteria is met for the Kuramoto oscillators, but requires further analysis for the other types of oscillators. We have also investigated the application of our criteria to populations of oscillators that exhibit phase switching, such as in the case of the Rossler and Hindmarsh-Rose oscillators. Our research provides a clear and detailed understanding of the explosive synchronization phenomenon in populations of oscillators that are coupled and interact with each other. This knowledge can be used to improve the design of coupled systems that exhibit synchronized behaviour, such as engineering the optimal configuration of coupled lasers, rotary nanomechanicals, and chemical oscillators. We employ co-evolutionary genetic algorithms in a range of Cournot models to replicate players' learning behavior and assess their capacity for convergence to a Nash Equilibrium. A novel IA-based algorithm serves as the learning mechanism for individual players, adapting from a prior approach that utilized a method based on immunology. We examine how the properties of the search space and the characteristics of player types influence the outcome of the learning process, discovering that the new algorithm yields a more substantial share of equilibria across all search space conditions. Introducing a third best response player to the standard two-player Cournot game proves especially challenging for the learning algorithm, resulting in a significantly decreased likelihood of equilibrium convergence. Moreover, we find that the IA-based algorithm exhibits comparable performance when transitioning to the larger search space context, and successfully facilitates equilibrium convergence in a variant of the game that is purportedly intractable. Notably, the IA-based algorithm surpasses the efficiency of the previous immunology algorithm both in terms of execution time and number of steps required to reach an equilibrium, thereby holding the potential to provide valuable data in studies exploring the co-evolutionary learning of multiple equilibria games. Ultimately, we utilize statistical analysis along with visual embedding to gain a deeper understanding of the outcome of the learning process, revealing that the novel IA-based algorithm generates a more diverse population that is better adapted to the search space compared to the previous algorithm. This, in turn, leads to a greater diversity of equilibrium solutions and an increased capacity for convergence to a Nash Equilibrium. Additionally, we explore the concept of a player 'type' based on the structure of the search space, proposing a framework that may be applied to other multi-equilibrium games. We experimentally validate our approach using both synthetic and real-world data, encompassing over 30,000 individual player learning pathways in a variety of search space conditions. Our methodology allows for the assessment of a co-evolutionary genetic algorithm's capacity for achieving a Nash Equilibrium in a Cournot game across three main dimension: the structure of the search space, the characteristics of player types, and the design of the algorithm. Mobile devices equipped with visual-inertial odometry sensors pose significant challenges in indoor localization due to their limited and unpredictable sensor data, intense computations required for deep learning models, and the difficulty of training models for unknown environments. Existing VIO-based methods typically employ matching techniques to track places, but they are often prone to errors caused by incomplete memory, inconsistent data, and environmental changes. To address these issues, we propose an external memory attention learning framework, integrated with a robust optimization framework, to efficiently utilize memory resources, accurately match and synch temporal VIO data, and handle missing or inconsistent inertial signals, especially effective for mobile devices localized in indoor areas. Our method is comprised of two main components: an inertial initialization network that estimates the memory's starting point and synchronizes VIO data; and a visual optimization network that leverages the memory to search for the best local maximum under dynamic lighting conditions. Our method demonstrates superior performance and efficiency in various localization experiments using real VIO data, outperforming state-of-the-art deep learning models and VIO systems in terms of precision and computation requirements. Throughout a solar-type main sequence star's lifetime, its rotation gradually slows down, ultimately reaching a differential rotation similar to that of the Sun. However, in some cases, especially for stars spinning at half the solar rate, the differential rotation takes a contrasting form - often referred to as 'anti-solar'. In this type, the equator rotates faster than the poles, presenting an intriguing variation that has been observed in approximately twenty percent of solar-like prototype stars. A distinct characteristic of the solar-type dynamo is the generation of poloidal magnetic field from the toroidal field via flux emergence. If the solar-type dynamo is located near the base of the convective zone, as indicated by global magneto-seismology, a review of the effect of anti-solar differential rotation on this flux transport dynamo reveals that it results in the production of magnetic field patterns incompatible with the observed stellar characteristics. Consequently, a longer solar-type protostar lifetime is required for the emergence of magnetic cycles, with additional constraints imposed by the generated magnetic field patterns on stellar properties such as polarization levels and stellar brightness variations. For protostars with initial rotation rates similar to that of the Sun, the absence of anti-solar differential rotation allows for magnetic cycle generation as early as during the final stages of the protostar phase. One major challenge arises from microwave radiation used in circuit operation, which can induce damage through thermo-mechanical stress. We employed terahertz near-field scanning optical microscopy to non-invasively investigate the local heating and mechanical stress near areas of high electromagnetic stress in co-planar microwave resonators. We were also able to observe the recovery process of the resonator after it had been subjected to high power microwave radiation, indicating that the near-field terahertz scanning technique has the capability to monitor the condition of superconducting quantum circuits effectively.  This study's findings have implications for evaluating the state of other microelectromechanical devices used in microwave applications.  We also explored the possibility of employing this technique to detect subtle changes in the state of superconducting components, such as the transition from a superconducting state, which could be an interesting direction for future research.  We believe that near-field terahertz scanning has the potential to become an essential tool in the development of robust superconducting quantum circuits. This study employs a motivic perspective to examine curved K-theory, a homology theory derived from algebraic K-loop constructions. Initially, we establish the representability of family functoriality for curved K-theory in the context of relative motives. Subsequently, we utilize this result to demonstrate that curved K-theory possesses a Grothendieck duality property, following a pattern observed in classical algebraic K-theory. Notably, we achieve this conclusion without relying on Quillen's Periodicity Theorem. Moreover, we identify the motivic curved K-group of a variety X as the zeroth homotopy group of a motivic spectrum associated with X and a family of line bundles, establishing this connection through the use of motivic complete homology functors. Finally, we verify that curved K-theory exhibits part of the Murray-Christensen universal property in the context of motivic homotopy theory. This approach facilitates an extension of curved K-theory to a homological theory compatible with geometric morphisms. Ultimately, we relate curved K-theory to motivic spectral curves and algebraic stacks via the use of geometric localisation functors. This research is further illustrated by computations of curved K-groups for varieties of abelian schemes, K3 surfaces, and projective lines. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between curved K-theory and motivic cohomology through the application of Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer scenarios to elliptic curves. Lastly, we explore connections between curved K-theory and motivic L-functions, including the derivation of rational points on modular elliptic curves via curved K-theory. This research is further enabled by the capabilities of the Homotopy Type Theory (HoTT) proof assistant, which enables the construction of curved homology theories and associated geometric structures via dependent type theory. This perspective on homological theories as dependent types offers a novel avenue for their study. This study is further enabled by the presence of an institutional repository containing the HoTT proof assistant code employed in the research, which is made available under an permissive licence with no copyright restrictions. This approach to the study of curved homology theories as dependent types has implications for potential applications in the field of homological algebra. This study is a culmination of the author's doctoral research under the supervision of Peter Landau. This work explores possible atmospheric developments of Venus over millions of years, examining how internal processes such as effusion volcanism, surface interactions between rocks and gas, and chemical reactions within the atmosphere could have shaped its current composition. We also consider the planet's slow cooling interior and its impact on geological activity and atmospheric gas exchange between the surface and space. Our modeling indicates that the atmosphere may have developed through a balance between rock-gas reactions releasing carbon dioxide, counterbalanced by sulfuric acid rain removing CO2 from the atmosphere and decreasing volcanic activity over time. However, this equilibrium was disrupted when the interior cooled enough to allow magma with low sulfur content to reach the surface, increasing volcanic CO2 emissions and compressing the atmospheric sulfuric acid rain cycle, resulting in the highly corrosive atmosphere seen today. This outcome may not be unique to Venus; any planet with a slow-cooling interior and sulfurous surface materials could experience a similar atmospheric disruption. We propose future observations aimed at verifying our theoretical findings and assessing the planet's surface and atmospheric processes. This study was conducted as part of the Venus Research and Analysis Program (VRAP) and contributed to the scientific basis for the NASA DAVINCI+ and ESA UVES missions. Our modeled atmospheric developments could have implications for the potential habitability of Venus over time, while also offering insights into the planet's complex interconnections and the crucial role its internal processes play in shaping its surface and atmosphere. We examine how these processes interact with each other and the atmosphere in detail, while also outlining the key uncertainties in our current understanding of Venus's atmosphere and the improvements that will come from further data collection. Those improvements in turn could provide a better scientific basis for interpreting the data collected by the DAVINCI+ and UVES missions, providing a more comprehensive view of how Venus's atmosphere varies across the planet and between different time periods, while also enhancing our understanding of the complex relationships within this atmosphere and the processes that have such a significant impact on the surface from above. To this end, a novel technique called reaction nanoscopy is developed, allowing for the real-time, three-dimensional observation of particle formation. In this study, droplets of glycol with a sub-wavelength size are used as a model system to investigate the formation of ions resulting from photochemical reactions within these droplets. Utilizing the reaction nanoscopy technique and results from additional experiments, it is shown that the formation of these ions is highly dependent on the intensity of the laser and droplet size, ultimately resulting in either bimolecular reactions within the droplet or the extraction of an electron from glycol molecules by laser light. Furthermore, specifications for droplet and laser parameters are established in order to achieve a specific process of ion formation. Additionally, the applicability of this knowledge is demonstrated by applying it to the formation of nanoparticles within these droplets. Point processes that take into account multiple types of events, such as natural disasters, online messages, or neuronal activity, are used extensively in various fields. A key statistical model for these point processes is the nonlinear Hawkes process, which can exhibit persistent behavior and calculate the instantaneous rate at which events of a particular type occur. This work delves into the assessment of nonlinear Hawkes processes using a Bayesian approach, which involves utilizing Markov chain Monte Carlo methods to estimate model parameters and conduct tests on the process's consistency. Furthermore, we demonstrate a widely applicable Bayesian evaluation framework for determining the goodness of fit, performing model selection, and comparing the plausibility of competing point processes. This framework is accompanied by a publicly accessible Python tool called NHPy, which facilitates the estimation of nonlinear Hawkes process parameters and the evaluation of the process itself. We showcase this approach by analyzing three distinct datasets, including real-world data on 2022 flood events, and our implementation is available on GitHub under the permissive MIT license. Our findings are also accompanied by detailed diagnostic results, which provide valuable insights into the properties and behavior of events in question. Ultimately, this work elevates the nonlinear Hawkes process to a fully falsifiable model, enabling scientists to evaluate its effectiveness in modeling complex event data. As high-power laser pulse capabilities increase, the limitations of traditional solid-state optics due to their restricted damage thresholds pose significant challenges, making the investigation of laser-plasma optics a pressing research need. We study a specific configuration involving a high-intensity linearly polarized laser pulse interacting with a varying density plasma column, and through particle-in-cell simulations, we reveal that the plasma can significantly alter the polarization of the laser, shifting it by as much as 90 degrees, while also amplifying the electric field by a factor of 20 within a 10-femosecond time frame. This effect is closely tied to the formation of a quasi-stationary "anisotropic filter" in the plasma, which relies on the critical density depth relative to the laser wavelength. We also observe that this phenomenon persists across various initial plasma conditions and is unaffected by the presence of electron motion within the critical density depth, although it does rely on the specific conditions of high intensity and short duration. Notably, this discovery holds implications for the development of novel laser-plasma based optical components, as demonstrated through the application of this phenomenon in a proposed layout for a laser pulse polarization shift component. We explore the potential for such a component to process multiple petawatt laser pulses within a 10-femosecond time frame, a critical duration for many high-field science experiments, while also highlighting the associated challenges that arise with the increased power levels. This result enables us to re-evaluate the electromagnetic form factor of the tau lepton, leading to a revised determination of the tau lepton's electric dipole moment. Our new methodological approach differs from the conventional effective theory technique. Furthermore, we illustrate that the usual effective theory approach often yields an overestimation of the desired quantity. Our novel calculation yields a tau lepton electric dipole moment of $-173.95 i$, primarily driven by the W-boson contribution, in contrast to the conventional prediction of $-174.8 i$. This discrepancy arises from a distinct choice of integration contours in the complex energy plane. We advocate for the adoption of Jamin-Serre's rule to derive the relevant coefficient, which serves as a cross-check for our findings. Consequently, we establish an upper bound for the tau lepton electric dipole moment, namely $|d_{{\tau}}| < 2.46 \cdot 10^{-19}$ e cm, which is a more precise estimate than the current experimental limitation. Future experiments to study the Cosmic Microwave Background will be able to measure a crucial parameter $r$ with high precision, however a significant challenge lies ahead. Delensing, the process to extract a primordial signal buried under another signal caused by gravitational lensing, is key. To improve this process beyond traditional quadratic estimators which may not be sufficient, the next generation experiments could potentially benefit from more sophisticated methods such as a neural network that considers the full data set, leading to a significant enhancement in performance.

By comparing a variety of estimators including a new joint maximum likelihood estimator and neural network through extensive simulations representing future experiments such as CMB-S4, we demonstrate the potential of these methods to improve delensing across multiple scenarios including both high and low $r$ values. Notably, in scenarios where $r$ is relatively low, the delensing neural network shows a substantial improvement in the recovery of $r$, achieving an precision of $\chi^2/\mathrm{d.o.f.} \approx 0.1$ for $r=0.01$, a significant enhancement from the traditional quadratic estimator. Additionally, these methods show a considerable improvement in noise corruption, recovering $r$ with a precision of $\chi^2/\mathrm{d.o.f.} \approx 1$ for $r=0.01$, indicating that even in scenarios where the methods underperform in an ideal scenario without lens bias, they still offers a significant improvement in practice. Furthermore, we find that a variant of the neural network working directly with the delensing task achieves the best results, yielding a precision of $\chi^2/\mathrm{d.o.f.} \approx 0.1$ for $r=0.01$ in an ideal scenario and $\chi^2/\mathrm{d.o.f.} \approx 1$ in a scenario with a significant amount of lens bias and no foregrounds. Lastly, we explore the potential of these methods to further improve the delensing performance by incorporating additional information and techniques. We hope this study serves as a starting point for a broader discussion on the integration of machine learning techniques in the delensing process, a crucial step in unlocking the primeval information in the Cosmic Microwave Background. Additionally, the implementation of these methods will require a consideration of the statistical properties of the estimated parameters, leading to the derivation of accurate covariance matrices, a process we initiate in this study but recommend further exploration in future research. We obtained high-cadence photometric and spectroscopic data for SN~2020jfo in various wavelengths starting around day 3 up to day 363 after its explosion. SN~2020jfo, classified as a Type II with a short plateau duration, exhibited unusual characteristics in its light curves and spectra. During its initial plateau phase, SN~2020jfo's decline rate was abnormal, followed by a prolonged decline rate similar to that of other Type IIs. In spectra, a H-alphabalmer line with a distinctive double-peaked profile was observed, displaying a semi-empirical analysis similar to that of SNe with longer plateaus, although with some differences in ratio. A comparison with other Type IIs showed that SN~2020jfo's light curve and spectral features didn't match any other supernovae in our database, leading to difficulty in determining the progenitor's identity. A potential explosion energy or density variation or SN~2020jfo's unique pre-explosion environment could be responsible for its observed characteristics during expansion. A comparison with standard Type II supernovae light profiles showed a 100 erg/s/Hz larger $V$-band energy at day 25, along with a 10 K higher blackbody temperature, indicating SN~2020jfo's brightness and temperature during its plateau phase were similar to that of SNe with longer plateau periods. A nucleosynthesis analysis indicated that SN~2020jfo's explosion had approximately half the injected iron-peak elements compared to typical Type II progenitors, with variations in core size or mass, or pre-explosion drops in binary interaction rate possibly contributing to these results. A comparison with pre-explosion and broad-band light from SN~2020jfo's host galaxy at various wavelengths showed no signs of massive gas interaction or a circumstellar medium, contradicting the expectations based on SN~2020jfo's observed spectrum and light curves, or potentially an SN~2020jfo-like object in every 25 to 30 years. A Type IIb supernova explosion energy variation could also explain the occurrence of SN~2020jfo, potentially linked to a similar event in the X-ray afterglow, along with a dark companion star that could provide clues on SN~2020jfo's progenitor identity. A future study using the Hubble Space Telescope or a James Webb Space Telescope could help determine SN~2020jfo's absolute magnitude and provide a detailed analysis of its spectral features.
