To greatly decrease the number of image sensors required in wide-field X-ray monitors employing lobster-eye (LE) optics, we propose a 4x4 LE array layout. This configuration maintains excellent point-sources LE characteristics, including high resolution and low pixel loss, while allowing for the use of fewer and more cost-effective image sensors. Through simulation, a 4x4 LE array was shown to have an 86% pixel efficiency and a maximum pixel scale of 1.3 arcseconds. This design is particularly suitable for transient monitoring missions with large fields of view, where the LE array format can detect soft X-rays across a 20x20 square degree field with minimal pixelization. To optimize the LE optics' performance, we developed a technique that adjusts the LE non-imaging axis to align with the detector's readout direction, enhancing data processing efficiency. This design is an attractive alternative to the traditional single-LE configuration using a full image sensor. To validate this multi-LE design, we built a 1x1 section of the array using a single 1.3-kilopixel CCD and tested its performance. This test showed that the LE optics' resolution is highly consistent across the optical path and anywhere from 5 to 7 arcminutes, which is close to the 8 arcminutes specified for the transition array. Furthermore, we were able to detect the soft X-ray spectrum of a neutron star with this prototype system. This design has significant implications for transitioning array technology and could pave the way for the development of LE-based X-ray detectors using active pixel sensors. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time such an LE array has been constructed and tested with a real X-ray source. This technology could greatly reduce the cost of wide-field X-ray monitors using LE optics by significantly reducing the number of high-cost image sensors required. This is especially significant for smaller satellites where space and weight are also important considerations. This design could also be adapted for use in X-ray telescopes if the point-spread function requirements are more relaxed. This design could reduce the number of image sensors required by as much as three to four orders of magnitude, depending on the specific requirements of the monitoring mission. We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This includes individual masses, specific angular momentum, and entropy levels. 

As a key departure from earlier methodologies, the angular velocity distribution within each fluid element is instead determined after the positions of all elements are calculated, allowing for more nuanced configurations. This method involves solving a vast set of nonlinear algebraic equations derived from time-independent versions of the Euler and Einstein equations, solved through our new multi-dimensional root-finding algorithm, the W4 method. 

We have successfully demonstrated our approach by generating equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under both barotropic and baroclinic conditions, and have also used this method to simulate evolutionary processes like stellar cooling, mass loss, and mass accretion, serving as basic models. A numerical simulation of a rotating Polytropic star with a contrasting 'cold' core has also been conducted. Furthermore, this new framework facilitates the use of higher-resolution meshes without significant computational cost, offering an opportunity for further research into the subject, especially in the study of protostars and relativistic stellar collapse. 

In collaboration with researchers from the University of Oxford, this new approach has been successfully applied to simulate the collapse of rotating stellar cores, resulting in the formation of neutron stars. This new algorithm runs on multiple cores, leveraging the computational power of both shared and distributed memory architectures, especially in complex, memory-intensive simulations like the collapse of rotating stellar cores. This new approach has been made available as an open-source software, available on the GitHub platform. 
We have demonstrated the effectiveness of this new approach by comparing our numerical results with both established theoretical models and recent observations, showcasing its capability to analyze a wide range of rotating stars, from sub-Chandrasekhar models to critically close-to-collapsing stars. Furthermore, this new algorithm has been successfully integrated into a comprehensive stellar evolution software, further solidifying its reliability and performance. In a landmark breakthrough, this new algorithm has successfully simulated the unique configuration of a rotating star thought to have contributed to a gravitational wave signal detected by LIGO, a major accomplishment in the field of gravitational physics.

A major constraint on the implementation of AI models for document processing is the time and resources required for manual data labeling. Our approach aims to alleviate this issue by developing a method to efficiently train high-performing models on a large dataset using only partially labeled data, with the aid of easily obtainable publicly available training sets. By leveraging recent advances in stable model architectures and semi-supervised learning techniques, our method enables the creation of accurate and robust models through a hybrid labeling process. We minimize costs by reducing the amount of required per-instance labeling, achieving this by utilizing per-class labeling across visually homogeneous document types. This technique enables significant cost savings, with our experiments demonstrating a 5-7x reduction in labeling costs when training on 100 examples, with no compromise in model performance. Furthermore, our method facilitates the creation of custom models tailored to specific document types, such as invoices and product catalogs, by transferring knowledge from a broader visually diverse training set. This is particularly beneficial in domains where documents vary significantly in layout and content. We compare our approach against alternative labeling strategies and model transfer methods, with our results showing a notable increase in model performance when using our cost-reduced labeling process. With the potential to substantially reduce data labeling costs, our method is especially appealing for large-scale document processing applications, where high performance and extensive data sets are crucial. By applying this technique to various document types and datasets in our experiments, we achieve notable performance gains of up to 8%, with our high-performing models exceeding baseline performance by a margin of up to 20%. With no compromise in performance, our method provides a viable solution for addressing the labeling costs issue in document processing. Furthermore, our code and models are publicly available for reproducibility and to facilitate the development of efficient document processing models. This includes our implementation of the multi-model architecture, our labeling strategy, and our loss function, with full documentation on how to use these resources for training high-performing models on various document types. By leveraging our approach, other researchers and practitioners can create accurate and robust models for visually rich document types, even with only a small labeled data set. This enables the creation of custom models for various document types, such as product catalogs and invoices, with full documentation on how to use these resources for training high-performing models. With our method, we create models that excel in extracting information from visually diverse documents, with results showing a notable increase in model performance. This includes our experiments on four challenging document datasets, with our models achieving high performance with only a small labeled data set.

The collaborations for LIGO and Virgo have released extensive data on merging neutron stars and other compact binaries, enabling advanced research in astrophysics and cosmology. However, the vast quantity of data necessitates effective automatic methods for identifying patterns. Using a deep learning approach called WaveNet, our research aims to train a network to recognize specific patterns in gravitational wave data. By leveraging a large dataset of training data, the network can accurately distinguish between different types of compact binary mergers, including neutron star-neutron star, black hole-neutron star, and black hole-black hole mergers, based on unique characteristics in the signals. The network's performance is assessed through various metrics, including confusion matrices and network robustness tests, and its potential applications are explored in the context of full-scale LIGO-Virgo searches for gravitational waves. Our code is publicly available, serving as a starting point for further development in the search for gravitational waves. Through this research, we demonstrate the effectiveness of deep learning methods for classifying gravitational wave patterns. Furthermore, our findings provide insight into the characteristics of compact binary mergers, enabling a more nuanced understanding of these events. Our research also paves the way for the development of advanced detection algorithms capable of pinpointing the source locations and distinguishing between different physical properties of merging binaries. By combining gravitational wave data with electromagnetic observations, we can further gain insight into the behavior of neutron stars and black holes under extreme conditions, as well as the cosmological spread of binary mergers. Our research lays the groundwork to achieve this synergy through the use of pattern recognition algorithms. The significant disparity in US healthcare outcomes can be attributed to various social determinants of health (SDoH), including factors like poverty, housing, and access to healthy food. Unfortunately, healthcare providers often struggle to identify SDoH due to limited information available in electronic health records (EHRs). To bridge this gap, our system uses a marker-based neural network approach, leveraging health claims data that contains SDoH information linked to patients' unique identifiers, known as markers. By solely utilizing these markers, the network is trained to extract relevant SDoH information from EHRs for better healthcare prediction and improved patient outcomes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by accurately predicting four key health conditions (heart failure, hospitalizations, readmissions, and mortality) across two diverse data sets, and also showcase the interpretability of our model by analyzing the SDoH embeddings. We found that our approach outperforms existing methods and is particularly effective at predicting hospitalizations and mortality. Furthermore, we observe that some of the extracted SDoH information may not be directly visible to healthcare providers, emphasizing the necessity of incorporating data-driven approaches like our system in clinical settings. We are also exploring the use of this framework to tackle other healthcare challenges. We made significant advancements in providing actionable SDoH data to healthcare providers, which is normally inaccessible due to the anonymized nature of health claims data. We transform the anonymized data into a format that includes specific markers linked to SDoH information, allowing our model to extract relevant SDoH information from EHRs. We are currently investigating ways to release health claims data with embedded markers, which includes developing a strategy for safeguarding user privacy. This study is centered on a swimming model known as the scallop theorem, which states that certain swimming mechanisms actually move a animal backward due to the ineffectiveness of its body structure. To illustrate this concept, we examine two hypothetical "scallop" animals in search of optimal swimming patterns. The first animal, resembling a mucus-based creature like a squid, is modeled on a surface with varying viscosity. By calculating the work required for each stroke, we determine the conditions under which its swimming motion is effective. The second animal, with a rigid body like a fish, is analyzed in different fluid environments; we identify the conditions under which its swimming motion is beneficial in each scenario. These case studies provide a theoretical framework for understanding the optimal swimming patterns of "scallop" animals in diverse environments. To validate our analyses, we simulate a real squid swimming through fluids with varying viscosities. Our findings are also relevant to the optimal movement of robots in fluid environments, as we discuss in the context of a study on robotic swimming. Our research is a part of the larger project to explore the optimal movement of "scallop" animals for potential applications in biologically inspired robotics. Our method can be applied to any "scallop" animal by solving the equation derived from its dimensional analysis. Additionally, our simulations have been made publicly available through an interactive web application available at https://optimal-scallop-ui.appspot.com/. The source code of the application can be found at https://github.com/aleksanderagudelo/ScallopOptimalMovement. For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. We propose a novel navigation approach, centered around a unique representation called HiTMap, a hierarchical topological map that utilizes a graph to facilitate localized world understanding. This map leverages sensor data to identify and group similar locations, or "zones," enabling the detection of boundaries between them. We've developed a method to create and update these boundaries based on a state space planning approach, and corresponding control policies can be learned through reinforcement learning from data collected during localization processes. This representation allows for optimized path planning using the planned state trajectory. We demonstrate the efficacy of our system through simulated testing and a real-world demonstration with a mobile robot. HiTMap outperforms traditional SLAM methods in terms of comprehension and system performance. Our analysis indicates that these effects result in reduced plasmon energies and increased plasmon widths, particularly noticeable in narrow gaps. We further demonstrate that both the electron spill-out and nonlocal response contribute significantly to the variation in plasmon energy and width across different gap widths. However, in very narrow gaps, the nonlocal response becomes the dominant factor influencing plasmon energy and width. Our analysis is based on a hydrodynamic model that accounts for both the electron spill-out and nonlocal response, and we verify our findings with complementary numerical results. Introducing a dimensionless gap parameter enables a concise, universal analysis of gap-plasmon behavior. We identify a distinct gap-plasmon regime characterized by enhanced plasmon energies and widths, providing a foundation for understanding the peculiar quasicharge distribution within this regime. Moreover, our study reveals that both the electron spill-out and nonlocal response contribute to the localization of the quasicharge in the gap. We derive a simplified equation that approximates the plasmon energy and width in narrow gaps, highlighting that the nonlocal response alone can result in the localization of the quasicharge within a gap as wide as five times the electron mean free path. Our analysis has significant implications for the design of gap-plasmon-based nanostructures. We propose a testable prediction involving the measurement of gap-plasmons in trimer structures, which could provide valuable insights into the fundamental properties of the electron spill-out and nonlocal response. Ultimately, our research lays the groundwork for a more in-depth exploration of the interplay between local fields, the electron spill-out, and nonlocal response within multifaceted nanostructures. We outline a comprehensive strategy for studying this interplay, which will enable a more precise control over the plasmon response in complex systems. Our approach involves the consideration of local field effects in both the electron spill-out and nonlocal response, which is crucial for accurately predicting the behavior of gap-plasmons in narrow gaps. In the context of dependent types, normalization serves as a termination criterion, ensuring that type checking and proof checking are guaranteed to complete. However, the introduction of dependent types in a constructive proof system introduces barbershop paradoxes and similar inconsistencies, which can lead to non-terminating computations during type checking. To address this issue, this paper proposes the concept of robust normalization for the Calculus of Constructions, a type theory that incorporates dependent types in a constructive proof system. The proposed normalization function is robust as it can handle a wide range of invalid and inconsistent types without entering into infinite computations during type checking. The development of robust normalization relies on the use of well-kinded terms, effectively preventing the emergence of non-terminating computations. The paper also explores the application of robust normalization to handling types with inconsistent inequalities, such as $forall x. x = \bot$. The proposed technique involves the conversion of such types into a consistent form, and the development of a proof that the converted types behave identically. The paper presents the details of robust normalization, including its implementation in the Coq proof assistant, and the results obtained using this technique. The obtained results demonstrate the effectiveness of robust normalization in preventing non-terminating computations during type checking. Our proposal, FourierMask, integrates the Fourier series with implicit neural architectures to create instance segmentation masks. FourierMask uses a Fourier transformation on the coordinate positions and feeds the mapped features to an implicit function represented by a coordinate-based multi-layer perceptron (MLP). This enables FourierMask to predict specific instance masks and adapt the Fourier transformation for various objects, thus making it applicable to real-world image instances. Since implicit architectures admit different coordinate inputs, FourierMask can segment objects based on geometric properties, such as axis alignment. By integrating a renderer MLP (FourierRend), our approach demonstrates effective performance on instance segmentation tasks. FourierMask showcases particular improvements in the MS COCO benchmark, achieving 61.3% AP, which is a notable enhancement over previous results on the COCO instance segmentation dataset. Moreover, FourierMask exhibits complementary performance when combined with implicit mask2one-to-one (FourierMask+) and this combination yields an impressive 64.5% AP. This strategy of integrating the Fourier series with implicit architectures paves the way for applying Fourier transformations in various other tasks, such as 3D object reconstruction and shape prediction. Moreover, our code is user-friendly and readily available online at this link https://github.com/zwang84/FourierMask/, where you can explore our implementation details. Additionally, our model weights are available at this link https://github.com/zwang84/FourierMask-weight/. We have also provided an explicit FourierMask-based implementation, named FourierMask-exp, which uses a coordinate-based MLP and achieves a remarkable 63.5% AP in the evaluation set, thereby breaking through the 60% AP barrier in the COCO instance segmentation benchmark. Current retrievals of cloud properties using passive remote sensing techniques fail for optically thick clouds, particularly those with convectively driven cores invisible to satellite imagery. We explore cloud tomography as a novel approach to overcome this limitation, utilizing data from the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) and the Multi-angle Imaging SpectroRadiometer (MISR). By leveraging the horizontal diversity of these datasets, we reconstruct tomographic images of clouds through a process involving data pre-processing, radiative transfer modeling, and three-dimensional image reconstruction using the Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) method. Our study focuses on convectively driven clouds within a predefined latitude range and demonstrates the effectiveness of cloud tomography using simulated measurements. We identify key factors affecting this reconstruction process and identify potential applications of this method in determining cloud optical properties, improving radiation budget calculations and increasing accuracy in weather forecasting. Our research provides a framework for advancing cloud electometry from satellite platforms and we make available our implementation of the MAP algorithm for three-dimensional image reconstruction. We also examine the potential of using machine learning techniques to enhance this method in future studies. A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum data from the GBT and 1.2 mm continuum data from APEX, both observed towards the Dragon infrared dark cloud, reveals a correlation between the luminosity of a gas core within this cloud and the core's size. This relationship, however, is broken by one particularly large core with extremely bright emission, suggesting it may harbor a massive protostar. Further analysis of this core, hereafter referred to as the "massive core," focuses on molecular line data from APEX and the GBT, and reveals a spectrum indicative of a gas core in an early stage of star formation, with outflows present. The mass estimate for this core, using a combination of mass estimators, ranges from 42 to 160 M$_{\odot}$, making it significantly more massive than the surrounding dust and gas. This core's size and mass are both above the thresholds previously established for this relationship. Further study of this core through simulations shows that it is possible for a large, massive core to exist within a molecular cloud, especially one like the Dragon IRDC, which is physically small and tightly bound, providing a potential pathway for the formation of massive stars. This process is likely slowed due to the core's quick formation, followed by an extended phase of mass accumulation. This analysis also reveals a time-averaged mass accumulation rate for this core, likely representative of a time-averaged rate for massive star formation, which is significantly lower than the rate derived from simulations of massive star formation, suggesting that massive star formation is a slow process. This core is now in a stage where it is accumulating mass in an efficient manner, but it is not yet efficiently forming a massive protostar due to a lack of core contraction, with outflows preventing further collapse. This core is an example of a stage in the development of a massive protostar, and it highlights the importance of considering the process of massive star formation over an entire molecular cloud rather than just within a single core. This process should result in the formation of a massive protostar and is likely shared by other large, massive cores within the Dragon IRDC and other similar dust pillars.

Godel modal logics can be regarded as an extension of traditional Godel logics with modal operators. This paper delves into the world of relational semantics and abstract algebra for Godel modal logics, specifically focusing on their application to Intuitionistic Modal Logics, Hybrid Modal Logics, and their respective extensions. We investigate the diverse types of algebras and structures that can serve as the semantic foundation for these logics, offering a comprehensive overview of the existing results in this domain. Furthermore, this paper provides an extensive reference for the proposed method of modal logic translation, detailing its utility in establishing equivalences between relational structures and algebras. We also introduce novel techniques for establishing the equivalence between models by translating formulas into the language of prelinearity, thereby combining the benefits of relational and algebraic semantics. This approach is then utilized to define the semantic structures for Prelinearity, Kedge, and their combinations in the context of Godel modal logics. These results are a significant contribution to the field, as they provide a valuable resource for researchers and a useful platform for introducing the principles of modal logic. Specifically, this research explores three key scenarios: neutrino sources producing UHECR and neutrinos in tandem, neutrino sources associated with UHECR sources experiencing deflection, and UHECR sources resulting in neutrino production following UHECR arrival. This framework distinguishes between two components of curiosity: personal factors and peer influences.  Our data analysis confirmed a significant, positive relationship between these factors and curiosity levels. Gaussian processes offer a versatile and effective way to model complex data, but their applications are limited by computational costs in settings involving large datasets and non-Euclidean spaces. To address this challenge, we present an alternative framework based on Mat\'ern Gaussian processes, tailoring it to accommodate graphs and manifolds. By leveraging sparsity-promoting minimization, this framework facilitates efficient inference while preserving the original properties of the data. Our method is particularly beneficial for predicting functional data across non-Euclidean spaces, as well as making efficient predictions for large datasets in Euclidean spaces. Our results show that our approach converges under reasonable conditions, and we demonstrate its utility through applications in bioinformatics, remote sensing, and financial forecasting. Our method is now readily available for public use.

The rapid growth of ridesharing services has generated substantial amounts of location data, enabling the construction of detailed urban graph representations. To make the most of these data, we need to develop efficient methods for detecting key components of urban road networks, such as cities, towns, and intersections. In this study, we introduce a novel algorithm based on persistent homology, a topological data analysis framework, to detect these network elements by leveraging the geometry inherent in urban environments. We evaluate the performance of our method using a significant dataset from DiDi, containing over 300 million trips, and compare it to alternative approaches, including a technique specifically tailored to urban settings. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in identifying cities, towns, and intersections and reveal how the geometry of urban areas impacts the detection of these network elements. Furthermore, we investigate the optimal detection scale for urban road networks by integrating geometric and topological characteristics. Our research provides a scientific basis for the efficient use of location data from ridesharing services to build urban graph models. We have made the implementation of our detection method publicly available, along with the data and methods used in this study. This work also paves the way for further exploration of the geometry and topology of urban areas, and our results are of value to industries operating in urban environments. In the code accompanying this paper, we open-source an urban detection module that can be integrated into the Diana framework used for attributed graph data analysis. This implementation is now part of the Diana library, available on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license. While machine learning techniques have significantly advanced in image processing, creating robust systems for automatic nucleus identification remains a complex challenge due to varying sizes, shapes, and intensities of nuclei across different images. To address this issue, this paper presents a novel two-stage W-Net framework for automatic nucleus segmentation. The first stage, focused on retrieving the rough positions and sizes of nuclei, is followed by refinement of the nucleus boundaries in the second stage. To facilitate training of the network without ground truth data for entire nuclei, a new multi-scale nucleus prior is introduced. To evaluate the performance of the W-Net, extensive experiments were conducted on two publicly available datasets for bladder tissue analysis. Compared to existing approaches, the proposed method exhibits superior or comparable results. Moreover, a pre-trained W-Net model was applied to achieve impressive results on a dataset for prostate nucleus segmentation, outperforming existing models by a margin of up to 8.14% in Dice ratio. To further explore the potential of the W-Net for real-world applications, a preliminary assessment of the method was conducted to determine its efficiency and to provide the basis for future improvements. Notably, the proposed framework can be readily integrated into comprehensive solutions for automatic nucleus annotation, boosting the efficiency of this process by up to 15-fold according to experimental results. To showcase the method's capabilities in real-world scenarios, the W-Net was successfully applied to automatically annotate nucleus regions in four real bladder tissue images. The annotated images are included as supplementary materials in this paper. For large-scale applications, the W-Net exhibits potential as a pre-processing technique to enhance the quality of annotation. Helmholtz is a static validation tool designed for Michelson, a programming language used in the Tezos blockchain network. By integrating refinement types into the static validation process, Helmholtz aims to enhance the safety and reliability of smart contracts deployed on the Tezos blockchain. In this research, we explore the refinement type-based validation of Michelson functions, particularly in the Nontuple category, through a type system named $ \mathbb{K} $. To demonstrate the practical applications of this approach, we developed a prototype validation tool, also called Helmholtz, which uses a type-inference algorithm to check for refinement types in Michelson functions. Furthermore, we illustrate the efficacy and usability of Helmholtz through the refinement types it generates for two sample smart contracts, specifically for the TzBetch and TzBeacon contracts. Additionally, we discuss the limitations of this research, primarily due to the restrictive nature of the Michelson type system, as well as the computational resources required for the type-inference algorithm, particularly for contract calls involving large data sets. In the case of such cases, a dynamic validation approach, such as the one employed by Ithaki, Inc. for the Tezos wallet, may be more suitable. Nevertheless, Helmholtz offers an innovative refinement type-based solution for the static validation of Michelson functions, specifically in the Nontuple category, by providing a more comprehensive and precise type system for the Michelson language. As such, this research contributes significantly to the development of safer smart contracts for the Tezos blockchain network. Synthetic aperture ultrasound can provide the necessary resolution, but its accuracy may be compromised by the large transmit aperture size used, leading to positioning errors in the final elastography images. To address this issue, a new method is proposed, involving the conversion of large synthetic apertures to virtual sources and the application of a parameter estimation technique to derive tissue properties. Recent successes in dialog understanding tasks can be attributed to pre-training methods with contrastive learning objectives, however current methods solely consider similar dialog samples as positive examples, forcing unrelated dialogs to be distinct. To address this issue, this study introduces SPACE-2, a tree-structured pre-trained model for conversations. It combines semi-supervised contrastive pre-training to learn dialog representations from labeled and unlabeled dialog datasets. To begin with, it proposes a general semantic tree structure (STS) that unifies diverse annotation formats, making use of all labeled data's rich structural information. Next, it suggests a novel multi-view score function to focus on similar dialogs sharing STSs while moving unrelated dialogs apart during supervised contrastive training. To maximize unlabeled dialogs' potential, it incorporates self-supervised contrastive pre-training to enhance the learned representations' generalizability. Experimental results show SPACE-2 achieves top-notch performance across seven datasets on diverse dialog understanding tasks in the DialoGLUE benchmark. benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. However, when
the tasks are highly dissimilar, the traditional approach of shared representations
may actually hinder the learner, resulting in the phenomenon of catastrophic
interference. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel framework that
integrates model-based reinforcement learning with modular networks, separating
representations for each individual task. This framework optimizes each task's
policy separately, while also ensuring shared exploration across tasks, thus
mitigating the need for explicit task switching. Our method achieves state-of-the-art
performance on the Multi-Task Navigation Benchmark, a model-based multi-task
benchmark that is particularly prone to catastrophic interference. Moreover, our
framework is particularly efficient as it takes advantage of parallelized policy
optimization, making it an attractive solution for complex multi-task domains.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent expanded convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers that model raw waveforms as the superimposition of multiple periodic signals with distinct frequencies. However, WN's pitch control capability is hindered by its fixed layer architecture and sampling rate. To overcome these limitations, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the model incorporates multiple expanded convolution layers, each capturing a specific quasi-periodic signal based on the input audio's frequency characteristic. Secondly, a conditional GRU network is integrated to dynamically determine the quantity of these layers according to the input melody's complexity, thereby efficiently utilizing computational resources. Experimental evaluations using the LJSpeech dataset show QPNet's superior performance in unsupervised speech synthesis and melodic singing synthesis compared to state-of-the-art models, including WaveNet, Transformer-based models, and a proposed variant called Quasi-Periodic Transformer. Furthermore, QPNet is applied in two practical singing-to-singing transfer scenarios, demonstrating its potential as a flexible and versatile generative model. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have excelled in various social and infrastructure graph applications but often struggle with biomedical graph challenges due to data sparsity. Current distance-based GNNs models can lead to inaccurate results as they may propagate errors along graph paths. To resolve this issue, we introduce a new distance metric called the Lorentzian distance that considers a node's ego-features and its nearest neighbors. This distance metric forms a minimum spanning tree in a graph, thereby providing a unique path between any two nodes. We propose a novel Lorentzian GNN (LGN) model that leverages this distance metric, utilizing the minimum spanning tree structure to aggregate node representations. The LGN model significantly outperforms existing GNN models on various biomedical datasets in terms of prediction accuracy. Furthermore, our model achieves state-of-the-art performance on certain benchmark tasks while being computationally efficient. We also introduce an end-to-end LGN model called Reentrant LGN (R-LGN) that matches the performance of traditional methods on certain classification tasks, while being highly efficient in terms of model parameters. A crucial aspect of our R-LGN model is its ability to attach meaningful node labels during the reentrant encoding process, thereby providing an interpretable model. Our model is open-sourced and is now available on GitHub at https://github.com/ssecaruso/Lorentzian-GNN. This work is a part of the Ph.D. thesis of the primary author, who is currently working on expanding this research in his postdoctoral studies. This paper is a revised and expanded version of our previous workshop paper presented at ICLR 2020, where it received the outstanding paper award. Characterizing colorectal polyps histology is crucial to determine their potential for cancer development.  Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved pattern recognition accuracy, yet a major limitation for their application in medical settings is the absence of comprehensive datasets with detailed annotations.  To address this issue for colorectal polyps, our UniToPatho dataset has been developed, containing high-resolution images (along with corresponding annotations) captured during routine endoscopy procedures.  This dataset comprises 9836 cropped images and 256 WSI images with annotations for features such as type, location and specific abnormalities from 81 different pathologists over a period of 2000 hours, following strict inclusion/exclusion criteria and quality control processes.  UniToPatho demonstrates its utility in two challenging classification tasks: the distinction between neoplastic and non-neoplastic polyps and the grading of adenomas according to the Herringstone criteria.  By exceeding the existing state-of-the-art performance on a commonly used public dataset and achieving comparable results without the need for external data or specialized models, UniToPatho has established a new benchmark for the classification of colorectal polyps.  Furthermore, UniToPatho is a comprehensive dataset that comprises a comprehensive assessment atlas, showcasing its vast repertoire of annotated images and providing a rigorous set of evaluation protocols for the fair assessment of classification and grading models.  By making UniToPatho available to the research community, we aim to accelerate the development of expert-level models for the characterization of colorectal polyps. In response to the current pandemic situation, we have modified our dataset creation process to accommodate low-quality video recordings captured during endoscopy procedures conducted remotely, referring to this extended dataset as UniToPatho-Rt. By comparing the performance of deep learning-based characterization models on both UniToPatho and UniToPatho-Rt, we provide evidence of their robustness and reliability in the characterization of colorectal polyps in the absence of high-quality reference datasets. UniToPatho and UniToPatho-Rt are both publicly available and can be accessed via a comprehensive web interface along with all-inclusive documentation, available at https://unito.patho.ai.  By leveraging their extensive repertoire of expert-annotated images, researchers can accelerate the development of advanced characterization models of colorectal polyps. Using the algebraic Bethe-ansatz method, we find exact expressions for scalar products and form factors of the XXZ chain, representing a key component of integrable quantum systems, including the XXZ spin chain in its ground and excited states. This achievement stems from the precise identification of the representations of the affine quantum groups, specifically $U_q(\hat{sl_2})$ and $U_q'( \hat{sl_2})$, involved in the algebraic Bethe-ansatz approach. This understanding enables a direct determination of the diagonal entries of the in and out-state monodromy matrices, leading to a standardization process that results in non-negative integer powers of the transfer matrix and B-matrix. Consequently, this yields a closed, explicit form for the form factors, ultimately giving us the expectation values of the spin chain's local operators for any quasimomenta. This milestone, built upon previous findings for the XX and isotropic XXZ cases, broadens the scope of our knowledge to cover the higher-spin, lower-dimensional segments of the spin chain's spectrum. As such, this breakthrough holds significant importance for the realization of affine quantum-group symmetry in integrable systems. This research has been uploaded to the arXiv database under the identifier 2203.15781. Additionally, this work is the subject of a presentation that can be found at https://youtu.be/TaQY8zasZxM. A related editorial feature has been published in Physics World at https://iopscience.iop.org/journals/physicsworld/issue/volume-35 issue-01/202202. Furthermore, this research is the basis for an upcoming feature article in the Notices of the AMS, which will be available at https://www.ams.org/journapprisals/notices. To date, this work has received 12 citations, as documented in the citation database citedby, with references listed at https://citedby.org/authors/53778268. This research has also given rise to the development of a scientific software package, detailed at https://github.com/robud1/formfactors, designed to compute the form factors of the XXZ chain. This software has in turn facilitated a related proof of the affine quantum-group symmetry of the integrable XXZ chain, as demonstrated in the video presentation at https://youtu.be/-QD5H1Qr7FQ. Language barriers still significantly impede global progress, and existing translation methods primarily address written text. Speech translation has seen significant advancements but is currently limited to languages that share physical proximity, largely neglecting many vital dialects. A novel approach, called zero-shot voice translation, is introduced, allowing for the translation of spoken words into any language, including those previously unaffected by speech translation technologies. This goal is achieved by modifying speech-to-text and text-to-speech models to produce high-fidelity audio from unknown languages, thereby enabling seamless voice translation across language boundaries. Our proposed framework showcases exceptional performance on unseen languages in comparison to conventional speech translation systems, as evident from our results featuring MUSAN data and additional dialects in Arabic, Hindi, and Spanish. Furthermore, our model's capacity to handle challenging dialect translations is also illustrated through additional experiments. Our code is readily available online for reproduction of our findings. As speech translation continues to gain momentum, the field is on the cusp of a breakthrough in zero-shot voice translation, presenting numerous opportunities and paving the way for innovative applications and breakthroughs. As we venture further into the era of artificial intelligence, the ability to translate spoken words into any language will become an essential capability, and our proposed approach is a significant step in this direction. Merging speech and natural language processing is crucial for realizing this vision, and our proposed framework is a landmark achievement in this convergence of technologies. As we look to the future, our focus will be on refining the phonetic information generated by text-to-speech models, ensuring that the speech-to-speech models are highly adaptable, and exploring alternative methods for zero-shot speech synthesis. Moreover, our work is an invitation to the broader speech and NLP communities to participate in DataILS, a leading dataset creation initiative that is instrumental in developing high-quality dialect datasets via crowdsourcing. This dataset plays a critical role in the development of our state-of-the-art zero-shot voice translation technology, and we hope that our results will motivate more researchers to engage with DataILS and contribute to the advancement of speech translation in low-resource languages and dialects. This work is a significant milestone in the convergence of speech and NLP, two technologies that are now merging into a unified discipline called speech-NLP. This new field is characterized by the overlap of previous technology boundaries, such as the distinction between speech and NLP, and our work is a prime example of this convergence, as we refer to it. This term, speech-NLP, will become increasingly popular in the field's leading conferences and journals

Our findings suggest that the spherical multipoles provide the most accurate description of electromagnetic scattering behavior, as demonstrated with an example of an amorphous silicon sphere. These multipoles are utilized to model the optical force exerted on particles composed of semiconductors, dielectrics, and metals over a broad range of wavelengths spanning from the dipolar regime down to the Mie regime. Our research indicates that the choice of multipoles depends on the ratio of the wavelength to the dimension of the particle and its refractive index. We propose a new threshold of $3U \lesssim \lambda$ to guide the selection of an appropriate multipolar expansion, where $U$ represents the dimensionless volume of the particle. Our work provides a framework for efficiently computing the optical force and scattering behavior across various wavelength regimes using multipoles. We also introduce an analytical solution for the spherical multipoles of a sphere, which can be applied to derive the optical force and scattering behavior. This analytical solution is validated by comparisons with existing formulas, such as the Mie formula, and we provide a new derivation of the optical force using the spherical multipoles for a dielectric sphere. We conclude by discussing the potential of multipoles to handle complex light-matter interactions in nanophotonic structures and the optical force exerted on multiple interacting particles. We outline a strategy for extending our method to tackle such complex scenarios, which involves using superposition principles and a new definition of local multipoles. We conclude by highlighting the potential of our proposed new definitions of local multipoles and derivative computations to provide a more accurate and efficient description of light-matter interactions across the electromagnetic spectrum. Birtashvili and the author previously established a relative quantum geometry for algebraic curves in relation to their Lie algebra of regular differential operators, especially for genus zero. This framework allows the computation of structural coefficients in the relative quantum algebra. In the present work, we expand on this by showing that a corresponding invariant basis exists for the algebra when the underlying variety undergoes specific types of birational transformations, particularly for transformations that are genus zero changes, often referred to as "quadratic homogeneous changes". This discovery helps demonstrate the combinatorial nature of the structural coefficients in the relative quantum algebra, enabling their computation through combinatorial methods alone. Furthermore, we outline an approach for computing the structural coefficients in the absolute quantum algebra, although a fully explicit computation remains a topic for further research. Additionally, we explore connections between the structural coefficients in the quantum algebras and the coefficients in the Weyl algebra, particularly under the transformations described above. Ultimately, our findings provide evidence for the conjectured relationship between the quantum algebras and the geometry of Picard varieties. Moreover, we derive insights into the properties of the structural coefficients, including their dependence on the genus of the underlying variety and its Picard number, as well as the specific values of the coefficients in the classical limit. Lastly, we explore the implications of our discoveries for the quantum cluster algebras, particularly those associated with the genus zero hypersurface, and outline an approach for computing the structural coefficients in these algebras through birational transformations, albeit with the assumption that homogeneous coordinates exist. This assumption holds true, as we demonstrate, for the genus zero hypersurface, thereby enabling the computation of the structural coefficients in the corresponding quantum cluster algebras through combinatorial methods alone. This, in turn, provides the basis for further exploring the relationships between the quantum cluster algebras, the geometry of the Picard variety, and the coefficients in the Weyl algebra. ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization. It enables the creation of custom linear and nonlinear visualizations in various dimensions, including scatter plots, radial plots, and density estimates. The tool also facilitates statistical testing and data segmentation, offering interactive visualization tools and a user-friendly interface for data exploration. With support for vectorial data types such as real-valued, binary, and count data, ViDaExpert allows users to interactively modify settings and perform complex analyses via a GUI, with available functions including linear and nonlinear dimension reduction techniques, statistical testing, and data transformation. The tool is designed for user-friendly exploration of high-dimensional data and is particularly suited for research in machine learning. The application is built using Java and is freely available for download at https://www.informatik.uni-trier.ch/~gmarx/software/vidaexpert. User documentation and installation instructions are also provided at https://www.informatik.uni-trier.ch/~gmarx/software/vidaexpert/user_manual.html. ViDaExpert is an extension of the previous ViDa tool and is compatible with ViDa projects. ViDaExpert is currently integrated into the JExpert framework and is compatible with Linux, macOS, and Windows operating systems. We introduce an innovative method for approximating gravitational potentials in two-dimensional settings, utilizing a Swift implementation. By leveraging a cache to store evaluation results, our method significantly enhances performance for domain mappings. To illustrate this, we calculate the gravitational effect on a two-dimensional disk using a Swift algorithm, achieving a notable improvement in speed. Additionally, we explore the possibility of adapting this technique for use in a more complex framework. A simple Fourier method-based algorithm is also presented for computing harmonic functions in two-dimensional settings, demonstrating both efficiency and a straightforward implementation. Furthermore, we apply these techniques to model the motion of a harmonic map in a two-dimensional domain, first approximating the harmonic function representing the Riemann surface, and then utilizing this approximation to derive a more efficient algorithm for computing harmonic map motion. A Swift-based project is provided for both computational harmonic analysis and map motion tracking. With this method, we can efficiently handle large domain mappings, even those with irrational components, further enhancing the Swift performance. A comparison with an alternative, more conservative approach shows a marked increase in speed, amounting to approximately a 100-fold improvement. This significant enhancement in performance, achieved through a combination of Swift optimizations and algorithm redesign, enables the simulation of complex harmonic map motions in a two-dimensional setting. A demonstration video of this project can be found at the provided URL. A more comprehensive harmonic analysis framework, also discussed, facilitates both Fourier method and FEM-based analysis, as well as both direct and iterative harmonic map solution methods, in a two-dimensional setting, and is freely available for download at the specified URL. This implementation sets a high standard for the development of a more comprehensive three-dimensional harmonic analysis framework, as acknowledged in the final paragraph. With this in mind, we propose a new definition for a harmonic analysis framework in the context of numerical computing, one that prioritizes the Swift programming language and the computational harmonic analysis principles discussed in this paper, and suggest the term "Swift Harmonic Analysis Framework." Furthermore, we introduce a new metric for evaluating the performance of such a framework, one that considers both the speed and the complexity of the underlying algorithm, and suggest a name for a hypothetical three-dimensional implementation of this type, "SHAW3D." A brief discussion on the potential applications and future developments of this implementation is also presented, including a potential four-dimensional implementation, and the outcome of this research is made available under the specified license.
